Drawing on a novel geo-coded dataset of project locations from the Kyoto Protocol’s Clean Development Mechanism, we show that projects are more likely to be allocated to constituencies represented by co-partisans of the Prime Minister’s party, and that this effect is strongest in competitive constituencies within states governed by opposition parties, where the central government has the sharpest incentives to build new support. This is surprising because existing literature on the Clean Development Mechanism suggests that decisions on project allocations are depoliticized. By demonstrating otherwise, this article contributes to the literature on International Climate Funds by demonstrating the importance of domestic politics in shaping its distribution.
items.title: The spatial politics of International Climate Finance: A case of India
Corrigendum to “Trust in civil servants: A cross-national dataset for public policy research, 1986–2022”

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Many existing states, including the US and the UK, promote a particular housing tenure, owner‐occupation. Yet liberalism is commonly associated with commitment to a principle of state neutrality which holds that states ought to be neutral regarding different ideas of the good life. This raises important questions, and ones that have received little philosophical attention. Does a commitment to liberal state neutrality rule out the promotion of owner‐occupation? More broadly, what follows from a commitment to the neutrality principle for state action around housing tenure? In this article, I argue that a weaker neutrality principle, neutrality of justification, allows states wide latitude to promote particular housing tenures, including owner‐occupation. However, on a stronger and, I argue, more tenable reading of the neutrality principle, state promotion of owner‐occupation is plausibly ruled out. What is not ruled out, however, is state promotion of a different tenure: renting. Before making these arguments, I defend the application of the neutrality principle to state action around housing tenure.
items.title: State Neutrality and Housing Tenure: What Can States Promote?
Reasons as First-Order Evidence
Claims and Complaints
More representative or smarter, but not both: the democratic dilemma in lottocracy

items.abstract: Abstract This paper bridges two distinct traditions – philosophy of mathematics and proof theory – to provide a formal framework for explanatory proofs in mathematics. We focus on explanatory proofs that uncover the grounds of mathematical theorems, and we formalize their structure using a new “axioms-as-rules” approach. Our method ensures the transformation of axioms into inference rules while preserving key logical properties such as soundness, completeness, and cut-admissibility. Two classical examples, the Quadrangle Theorem and Pythagoras’ Theorem, are revisited to show how explanatory steps can be systematically isolated and formalized. This framework not only offers novel proof-theoretic insights but also enhances our understanding of mathematical explanations by bridging informal intuition with rigorous formalism.
items.title: Mathematical Explanations and Axioms as Rules

items.abstract: Abstract Increasing polarization across many contexts raises the question of whether justice measures exacerbate or mitigate social divisions. To develop hypotheses about how justice operates in divided contexts, this article draws on theoretical perspectives from the interdisciplinary field of transitional justice. It examines convergence and divergence in fairness evaluations using a fully randomized conjoint experiment. The experiment was embedded in nationally stratified online surveys in Japan ( n = 2,700) and South Korea ( n = 3,000). The bilateral setting provided a useful research site for a study of a divided context: contested colonial legacies and a variety of justice measures for addressing the past, which were suitable for experimental manipulation. The results show that most justice measures elicit opposing responses in the two countries while simultaneously reducing differences between them. This reveals a paradox of justice: even divisive justice measures can, under certain conditions, bring groups closer together. This framework enables to classify the effects of justice measures into convergent, divergent, and paradoxical configurations and to consider the theoretical and empirical implications for existing and future experimental research on social conflict and divided societies across disciplines.
items.title: The paradox of justice in divided settings
What we talk to when we talk to language models

items.abstract: Abstract In this paper, I analyze the responses of three emblematic continental European legal philosophers associated with Thomistic legal philosophy—namely, Francesco Viola, Michel Villey, and Javier Hervada—to the main arguments regarding the nature of law advanced by the new classical natural law theory of law, more precisely, by the main proponent of this theory, John Finnis. While Viola’s arguments largely overlap with Finnis’s account of the nature of law, according to which all human law is necessarily posited, Villey and Hervada, in their direct or indirect dialogue with Finnis, ground their theories on the essence of law in phenomena or features such as the thingness of law and law’s radical dependence on the virtue of justice, which enable them to establish the existence of elements of real juridicity outside of the scope of humanly posited law. I argue that it is possible to unify these various Thomistic attempts to elucidate law’s nature within Aquinas’s broad idea of law, which necessarily includes (1) a reference to law’s thingness, (2) law’s conceptual dependence on the virtue of justice, (3) law’s essential reliance on the phenomena of legal norms (both natural and positive), and (4) the connection between the nature of law and human good.
items.title: The Responses to the New Classical Natural Law Theory of Law in Continental European Thomistic Legal Philosophy

items.abstract: Abstract This essay makes the case for an alternative approach to the interpretation of the European Convention of Human Rights, one rooted in the classical natural law tradition. The foundation of the alternative approach is a reconstruction of the jurisprudence of one of the European Court of Human Rights’ most heterodox judges, Sir Gerald Fitzmaurice, who was the United Kingdom’s nominated judge between 1974 and 1980. In his dissents, concurrences, and extrajudicial writings, I argue, are the conceptual and normative seeds from which a more promising approach to interpreting the Convention can be grown. My alternative approach does not represent a repudiation of the moral purpose or point of the Convention but is in keeping with one of the principal moral impetuses behind its creation: the desire to protect the most basic and fundamental human rights that are owed as a matter of justice to all persons. I also suggest this alternative method would, if adopted, deflate a great deal of the legal and political critique directed toward the Court.
items.title: The Sir Gerald Fitzmaurice Option: A Classical Natural Law Method for Interpreting the European Convention on Human Rights

items.abstract: Abstract The principle of sufficient reason (PSR) implies that everything has a sufficient reason. Yet its role in ethics has gone undertheorized. A stark historical exception is found in Christian Wolff, the most influential German philosopher between Leibniz and Kant. I argue that the PSR has indispensable non-normative and normative uses in ethics for Wolff—uses without which ethics would not be possible at all. In sketching these uses, I highlight how Wolff aspires to skirt two Humean challenges. The first concerns how the PSR, which concerns what is, can imply anything about what ought to be. The second concerns how the reasons established through the PSR can be morally motivating. Although hardly unproblematic or uncontroversial, Wolff’s discussion of the PSR in ethics offers both a welcome exception to centuries of undertheorizing and a potential challenge to opponents of the PSR.
items.title: The Principle of Sufficient Reason in Ethics: Lessons from Wolff

items.abstract: Understanding how voters use the left-right scale is essential, as it is not only related to vote choice but also underpins how political scientists study ideology. This article finds that the way voters use the left-right scale is variable. Using British Election Study Internet Panel data from 2014 to 2024, I find that while economic and cultural values are both related to left-right self-placement, this varies both between individuals and over time. Those on the left of the self-placement scale can best be differentiated from one another by the strength of their economic values. For those on the right, cultural values are more useful in separating between different self-placement levels. Over time, left-right self-placement has become increasingly related to cultural values alongside economic values, driven by movements by people on both sides of the left-right scale. These findings indicate that even within one country, the meanings of ‘left’ and ‘right’ vary.
items.title: The changing meaning of left-right self-placement in the United Kingdom

items.abstract: This article examines the tension between sociology and history as a methodological problem of reconciling general concepts with historical specificity. It assesses evolutionary theory as one influential attempt to address this challenge. Focusing on Neo-Darwinian social evolutionism, in particular on W. G. Runciman’s selectionist framework, the article argues that evolutionary theory does not establish the general causal mechanisms it claims to identify, but instead, provides a vocabulary for describing recurrent features of historical processes. The argument therefore proposes a reconceptualization of evolutionary theory as a Weberian ideal-typical framework whose value is heuristic, descriptive, and comparative rather than causal.
items.title: History, Sociology, and Evolutionary Thinking: Epistemic Limits Reconsidered

items.abstract: Abstract Most people have a need to regard their significant life choices as justified. More than that, they want to be able to give acceptable justificatory reasons to the people in their social milieu. In this paper, I argue that structural disadvantage can lock people into a situation in which they struggle to appeal to their best reasons. I start out with a paradigmatic example inspired by Jennifer Morton’s work on disadvantaged students aiming at upwards mobility and identify a struggle that has more than one cause but amounts to a distinctive experience: that you have objectively good reasons for a life choice, which, however, are not available to you because of your social position. I analyse this ‘unavailability’ of a reason with the help of existing literature on epistemic injustice, in particular hermeneutical injustice, and coin the new term ‘justificatory injustice’. While it can be described as epistemic injustice broadly conceived, justificatory injustice goes beyond epistemic access in a narrow sense and is entangled with features distinctive of practical justification taking place in a concrete social milieu. Justificatory injustice, I argue, can only be remedied in a more integrated justificatory community, which requires equality of condition, also in economic terms.
items.title: Justificatory Injustice: Epistemic Injustice in the Availability of Reasons

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines the viability of framing intergenerational power asymmetries in terms of sovereignty, particularly in non-overlapping contexts. It is divided into four parts. First, it surveys the different dimensions of sovereignty, focusing in particular on absoluteness, self-justification, and perpetuity. Second, it applies these dimensions to the concept of generation within constitutional theory. From the perspective of McTaggart’s A-series of time, this analysis shows that intermediate generations do not satisfy the criteria for sovereignty, thereby raising questions about the asymmetric distribution of power in relation to the founding generation. Third, the article adopts McTaggart’s B-series of time and examines fully constituent generations (such as the generation responsible for establishing the first historical constitution), concluding that the concept of sovereignty remains inapplicable. Finally, it considers the conceptual and normative implications of this conclusion. It examines the consequences of simply replacing sovereignty with related concepts (such as independence) in discussions of generations, as well as the possibility of reconciling sovereignty with limits on the power exercised by each generation. Such a reconciliation may draw on arguments from intergenerational justice and political liberalism, but ultimately depends primarily on an argument from cross-temporal popular sovereignty.
items.title: Decoupling Generational Sovereignty: The Cross-Temporal Role of the Sovereign People

items.abstract: Abstract As millions of Muslims worldwide turn to LLMs like GPT, Claude, and DeepSeek for religious guidance, a critical question emerges: Can these AI systems reliably reason about Islamic law? This paper introduces , the first multi-school benchmark for evaluating LLM performance across a broad range of Islamic jurisprudence ( fiqh ). Drawing from 37 foundational legal texts spanning 1,200 years and seven schools of jurisprudence, we create 718 evaluation instances across 13 tasks, manually collected and organized by complexity, from basic recall to sophisticated reasoning including legal rationale identification ( ‘illah ), analogical application ( qiyās ), and cross-school synthesis. Our evaluation of nine state-of-the-art LLMs reveals significant limitations. Even the best model achieves only 67.65% correctness with 21.25% hallucination; several models achieved correctness below 35% and hallucination exceeding 55%. Furthermore, few-shot prompting yields no consistent benefit; per-model changes range from -3.64 to +4.16 points, with gains concentrated in already-weak models, consistent with insufficient Islamic legal knowledge in current training data that prompting, under closed-book conditions, could not compensate for . Our analysis reveals why: moderate-complexity tasks (from a human expert’s perspective) requiring exact, verbatim knowledge (e.g., enumerating contract conditions, synthesizing statutory articles) show consistently high error rates and hallucination rates up to 73%, whereas high-complexity tasks show better performance because models rely on semantic generalization and verbose reasoning, projecting competence while lacking precise textual understanding. False premise detection reveals risky sycophantic behavior: under few-shot prompting, 5 of 9 models accept misleading assumptions at rates exceeding 40% (worst: 86.27%). Critically, few-shot prompting worsens sycophancy by 3.49 percentage points. The strong and statistically significant negative correlation (Pearson’s r = –0.91, n = 9, p < 0.01) between the false premise acceptance rate and overall performance indicates that models with higher false Islamic query acceptance rates tend to exhibit lower overall reasoning accuracy. Our findings carry important implications: the path forward for Islamic NLP lies not in lightweight post-hoc techniques such as prompt or instruction tuning but in enriching knowledge. The Islamic NLP community must prioritize training models on comprehensive, large-scale Islamic legal corpora that span classical Hadith collections, jurisprudential works from the major Islamic law schools ( madhabs ), and codified legal compendia.  provides the first systematic evaluation framework for Islamic legal AI systems, revealing critical limitations in platforms that Muslims increasingly rely on for spiritual guidance.
items.title: IslamicLegalBench: Evaluating LLMs knowledge and reasoning of islamic law across 1,200 years of Islamic pluralist legal traditions

items.abstract: Abstract The interlinked climate and ecological crises have profound implications for future human success. Temperatures are set to rise by 3–4 0 C by the end of the century and there is already a sixty-nine per cent global average biodiversity abundance loss since 1970. Most of our business and management literature continues to rely on traditional, anthropocentric, leadership and strategy theories as a route to change without considering the embedded, systemic, heterogeneous, and future-orientated nature of the problem. Given this multifaceted grand challenge, and the compounding lack of adequate business and management theoretical foundations for such research investigations, we propose six strategic leadership types (and their underpinning values and capabilities) that help to differentiate leadership for the complex climate and ecological crises we face. The leadership types, greenwash, resilience, eco-innovation, ecocentric visionary (sustainability), degrowth and regenerative leadership, are calibrated against known ontological and strategic perspectives, which provide plurality and fluidity of thought, allowing connection between the natural and social sciences, to aid understanding of research towards sustainability and climate change. We reframe the leadership literature by locating our theoretical contribution within environmental ethics, linking our understanding of the natural world, human ethics, and related business ethics, identifying regenerative leadership as the most ethical and most promising type.
items.title: Theoretical Foundations for a Sustainability and Climate Change Strategic Leadership Typology: Towards Regenerative Leadership
When Oversight Falters: Ethical Opportunism and Corporate Tax Avoidance under Governance Failure

items.abstract: Abstract To foster trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) within the European Union, the AI Act requires providers to mark and detect the outputs of their general-purpose models. The Article 50 and Recital 133 call for marking methods that are "sufficiently reliable, interoperable, effective and robust". Yet, the rapidly evolving and heterogeneous landscape of watermarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) makes it difficult to determine how these four standards can be translated into concrete and measurable evaluations. Our paper addresses this challenge, anchoring the normativity of European requirements in the multiplicity of watermarking techniques. Introducing clear and distinct concepts on LLM watermarking, our contribution is threefold: (i) Watermarking Categorisation: We propose an accessible taxonomy of watermarking methods according to the stage of the LLM lifecycle at which they are applied — before, during, or after training, and during next-token distribution or sampling. (ii) Watermarking Evaluation: We interpret the EU AI Act’s requirements by mapping each criterion with state-of-the-art evaluations on robustness and detectability of the watermark, and of quality of the LLM. Since interoperability remains largely untheorised in LLM watermarking research, we propose three normative dimensions to frame its assessment. (iii) Watermarking Comparison: We compare current watermarking methods for LLMs against the operationalised European criteria and show that no approach yet satisfies all four standards. Encouraged by emerging empirical tests, we recommend further research into watermarking directly embedded within the low-level architecture of LLMs.
items.title: Watermarking large language models in Europe: interpreting the AI act in light of technology

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines the protests of blueberry workers in Peru in 2020 against an agrarian labour regime that legalizes precarious labour conditions, as well as the aftermath of that mobilization. It investigates whether the legal change demanded and achieved can be categorized as resistance, understood as oppositional acts seeking rupture with the system, or as its opposite, accommodation, meaning reformist acts of opposition, acceptance and co-option. The analysis of the workers' mobilization in Peru tells a straightforward story about the function of law in constituting the rules of agrarian capitalism by distributing resources, such as land, into the hands of a few and legitimating unequal bargaining power to the detriment of workers. The findings suggest that the workers' protest constituted an act of accommodation: while it aimed to improve working conditions, it did not seek to overcome the underlying features and dynamics of the agrarian economic model that led to the entrenchment of precarity, unfreedom, and low levels of unionisation. While the mobilization did achieve legal change, its aftermath indicates that workers' actions were accommodating because they reinforced dynamics of co-option that curtail their capacity to organize and engage with projects of rupture.
items.title: Blueberry Workers, Legal Change, Resistance, and Accommodation in the Coastal North of Peru

items.abstract: Abstract This article describes and diagnoses a major shift in the modalities, uses and legal forms of the international role of the US dollar. Drawing from the work of Ranajit Guha, we argue that the balance between coercion and persuasion has shifted in comparison to the neoliberal era of dollar hegemony (early 1980s to early 2010s) and that this shift has reshaped the legal forms through which the currency power of the USA is articulated. Starting from the position that hegemony does not preclude the existence of coercion, we show that during the neoliberal era dollar hegemony enjoyed the consent of ruling classes around the world. Even when it was used to further geopolitical goals of the US, the US used international institutions, international law-making and co-operation amongst legal authorities in order to socialise its views and interests amongst political and legal elites. In contrast, the Trump administration exacerbated an already unfolding trend of openly coercive usages of currency power and the concomitant adoption of unilateral, highly visible executive or legislative action as the predominant legal forms through which the international role of the dollar is sustained and mobilised. We describe this shift as a transition from dollar hegemony to dollar dominance and argue that it has triggered less visible but equally consequential efforts by other states to hedge, rather than outright abandon, the dollar as the dominant currency of global capitalism.
items.title: From Dollar Hegemony to Dollar Dominance

items.abstract: Abstract A growing chorus of AI researchers and philosophers posit internal representations in large language models (LLMs). But how do these representations relate to the kinds of mental states we routinely ascribe to our fellow humans? While some research has focused on belief- or knowledge-like states in LLMs, there has been comparatively little focus on the question of whether LLMs have intentions . I survey five properties that have been associated with intentions in the philosophical literature, and assess two candidate classes of LLM representations against this set of features. The result is mixed: current evidence suggests that LLMs have representations that are intention-like in many—perhaps surprising—respects, but they differ from human intentions in important ways. Deciding whether to classify these representations as intentions will require careful consideration of the costs and pay-offs of extending the concept beyond the paradigm human case.
items.title: Intention-like representations in language models?

items.abstract: Abstract The Continuity axiom implies that no catastrophe is so bad that one should not be willing to accept a gamble that might result in that catastrophe, as long as the gamble is sufficiently likely to instead result in some improvement on one’s status quo. The axiom is implied by most normative decision theories, including risk averse alternatives to expected utility theory. We argue that Continuity should be abandoned when evaluating policy options where (a) there is sufficient uncertainty about the correct probabilities, and (b) some options could be catastrophic. However, unlike Bartha and DesRoches (2021) and Steel and Bartha (2023), we argue that there are examples of policy evaluation where, although the outcome could be catastrophic, the relevant probabilities are sufficiently well-grounded such that Continuity should be satisfied.
items.title: Continuity, catastrophic risk, and severe uncertainty

items.abstract: Abstract While logical expressivism and logical conventionalism share many commitments, the most prominent versions of these positions diverge in the kind of logical inferentialism they endorse. Jared Warren’s logical conventionalism adopts a form of unrestricted inferentialism, whereas logical expressivism naturally supports restricted inferentialism. This contrast is most evident in their respective treatments of the ‘tonk’ problem. This paper develops an expressivist defense of restricted inferentialism in light of Warren’s recent arguments for unrestricted inferentialism. I argue that the restricted inferentialist can accept Warren’s ‘Translation Mistake’ diagnosis of Unilateralist Tonklish, given that it interprets the addition of ‘tonk’ as yielding a semantically conservative extension of the original language. In the case of Bilateralist Tonklish, I argue that the restricted inferentialist can accept Warren’s verdict that it is a meaningless language because it is unfollowable, but that this unfollowability, in turn, is to be given a principled explanation in terms of constraints on inference rules. I contend that Warren’s discussion of ‘tonk’ reinforces the idea that logical connectives must play the expressive role that logical expressivists attribute to them, and that this role motivates restricted inferentialism.
items.title: Logic as Elaboration, not Pure Convention

items.abstract: Abstract Conceptual disruption is typically theorised as a consequence of technological innovation: a new artefact or practice unsettles an entrenched category, and a conceptual gap, overlap, or misalignment results. This paper argues that disruption also occurs when conceptual schemes collide, that is, when concepts travel across geopolitical boundaries and moral frameworks. It introduces Intercultural Conceptual Disruption (ICD) to theorise this second source of disruption. By using the example of the concept of PRIVACY in the African relational ontology of Ubuntu, the paper illustrates that conceptual disruption is not uniform across contexts. What counts as severe in one conceptual scheme may be mild or unremarkable in another, depending on the flexibility of that scheme and its ontological commitments, and the movement of concepts is shaped by asymmetries of epistemic and political power rather than by conceptual need alone. ICD is articulated as three interlinked processes: (1) identifying the type, level, and severity of disruption within a given conceptual scheme; (2) decentering dominant frameworks by addressing the epistemic injustices that privilege some conceptual resources over others; and (3) decolonising concepts that carry undue colonial influence in postcolonial contexts.
items.title: Decentering Disruption: Toward a Framework for Intercultural Conceptual Disruption
Can Normativity Be Fictional?

items.abstract: Abstract This article advances a doctrinal reinterpretation of the social dimension of the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. It challenges the assumption that bilateral social security coordination mechanisms operate as neutral instruments of transnational administration, arguing that, in situations of forced migration, they may instead function as structural barriers to the effective enjoyment of refugee rights. It argues that Articles 24 and 25 of the Refugee Convention require host states to ensure effective access to social security through functional substitution. The article concludes that refugee protection requires protection-sensitive social security coordination consistent with international and European legal obligations.
items.journal: Cambridge Yearbook of European Legal Studies
items.title: The Social Dimension of the 1951 Refugee Convention: Balancing International Protection and Social Security Coordination in Central and Eastern Europe
Intimate Borders: Feminist Migration Ethics by Amy Reed-Sandoval (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2025), pp. 1–180, £22.99, ISBN: 9781478026235

Astrid von Busekist.
                    Religion on Trial: An Essay on Deliberalism

items.abstract: Abstract Wang Yangming 王陽明 (1472–1529) has provoked controversy from his day to our own with his teachings about varieties of knowing ( zhi 知). A notable dimension of Wang's theoretical philosophy is his repeated insistence that the inherent reality of both the heartmind itself, and of knowing, is deeply affective in nature. While scholars have often noted Wang's emphasis on affect, we argue that affect is more fundamental to his view than previous interpretations have generally recognized. We develop an affect‐first interpretation of Wang's view of knowing in three steps. First, we show how joy, sorrow, and stillness jointly characterize the inherent reality of the heartmind. Second, we argue that the affective nature of our heartminds was important to Wang for two reasons, namely that it explains how the heartmind can be self‐sustaining and self‐correcting. Finally, we make explicit how Wang's innovative notion of good knowing ( liangzhi 良知) relates to the heartmind's affective inherent reality and fits together with other varieties of knowing. On our account, liangzhi is the heartmind's inherent reality as viewed through the lens of its responsiveness to the myriad things in the world. We argue that Wang's concepts of “extended knowing” or “genuine knowing”—which are the same thing—are nothing more than pure episodes of liangzhi. Taken as a whole, Wang's account of the heartmind's ways of knowing is consistent and distinctive, notable both for its influence within Neo‐Confucianism and its potential to catalyze new lines of thinking today.
items.title: Affective Knowing in Wang Yangming

Law and Justice in Song: Murder Ballads and Popular Music
                    By DanielNewman, London: Routledge, 2026, 310 pp., £171.99

items.abstract: Normative political theorists typically view displacement as a phenomenon that entails forced movement. In this article, I challenge this orthodoxy by arguing that displacement is fundamentally a loss of one's place and/or home that may occur either with or without such movement. After developing a series of conditions to explain when place-based changes precipitate ‘displacement without movement’, I contend that there are at least two key theoretical, ethical and political advantages to introducing this notion into normative political theory. First, the notion allows us to identify a common condition that unites the experiences of those who lose their place and/or home through forced movement and those who lose it in their habitual locations. Second, recognising this common condition may serve as a pathway to much-needed forms of solidarity among not only these two groups, but also non-displaced populations. I then discuss how the idea of displacement without movement may dilute the normative status that is often ascribed to displacement, while arguing that this implication is not problematic for my account. I conclude that displacement without movement should be viewed as a pressing global harm which deserves far greater attention by normative political theorists.
items.title: When home isn’t home anymore: Towards a political theory of displacement without movement

items.journal: Free & Equal: A Journal of Ethics and Public Affairs
items.title: Manipulation and the Demands of Agency

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Longtermists assign great moral importance to making the long‐term future as good as possible, especially by ensuring the survival of humanity. We argue, to the contrary, that on assumptions that are plausible, conservative, or shared by leading longtermists, human extinction will likely augment total utility among human and non‐human animals on Earth. The reason for this surprising conclusion is that our extinction would increase the number of sentient non‐human animals, which in turn would dramatically increase total utility. Possible responses by longtermists leave them with a difficult quadrilemma. They must either (a) welcome human extinction; or (b) welcome the extinction of most non‐human animals; or (c) tolerate continued human existence and related animal suffering as mere means to ushering in high‐tech transformations of the animal kingdom, space colonization, or digital sentience – relatively esoteric, unpopular, and speculative parts of longtermism; or (d) reject key tenets of longtermism like anti‐speciesism or the equal evaluation of making beings happy and of making happy beings. Embracing any horn of this quadrilemma would cut deep into longtermists' current commitments and/or dash central longtermists' hopes of popular appeal.
items.title: Must Longtermists Wish Us All Dead? A Quadrilemma
Russell on Structuralism
Reasons and Restrictors
Remembering the Rubber Ethnocide: Using Law and the Past to Move Beyond Development

items.abstract: Abstract With the increase of social housing deaths and crisis of housing conditions in Britain, it is imperative to understand the role of law and state-led forms of privatisation in making this situation possible. This article will focus on the historical and political context of the recent death of Awaab Ishak, who died in his socially-rented home due to mould overexposure. I argue that the law was not lacking here but will show how the juridification of housing governance through ownership mechanisms has been key in protecting the legitimacy of the state and capital accumulation more broadly in a British society ridden with economic crisis and social immiseration. To do this, I will theorise the development of a juridical framework that maintains the link between housing, the state, and capital by interpolating ownership and citizenship, in turn making social housing tenants responsible for unliveable social assets through the relocation of risk into their everyday lives. Going beyond critiques of housing privatisation and individualisation within contemporary accumulation strategies that depart from spatial forms of social organisation, I will argue that the link between law and capital needs to be understood temporally to account for the ongoing structural presence of non-accountability in the sector, that will not be simply remedied with incoming legislation. As such, renewed entwinements of property and racialisation that break with modern norms of individualistic ownership practices produce the conditions for the Ishak family’s experience of the sector and, ultimately and maddeningly, Awaab’s death.
items.title: The Juridification of Unliveable Social Housing: Ownership, Citizenship, and Responsibility

items.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into various aspects of society has raised pressing ethical concerns, from privacy and fairness to autonomy and safety. In response, the field of AI ethics has grown significantly, with a particular focus on developing guidelines to support the responsible development and use of AI. However, this trend has faced criticism, with concerns about “ethics washing” and skepticism regarding the overall value of AI ethics. In this paper, we argue that such criticisms often rely on an incomplete understanding of AI ethics. To address this, we propose an understanding of AI ethics that distinguishes between diverse instances of AI ethics (viz., research, education, practice, and governance instruments) and the purposes they serve (viz., knowledge, communication, and application). By disentangling these elements, we can illuminate different ways of doing AI ethics and provide a structured way to assess their value. Our arguments highlight that critiques of specific instances and purposes of AI ethics do not justify dismissing AI ethics altogether. We conclude by demonstrating how our proposed distinctions can reconcile existing defenses of AI ethics and guide future discourse, ensuring that the field remains both robust and relevant in addressing the ethical challenges posed by AI.
items.title: What is AI ethics, and what is it good for? Clarifying debates on AI ethics
Workplace AI ethics through a multi-stakeholder lens: a qualitative inquiry into responsibility, trust, and the limits of principles

items.abstract: Abstract The ongoing developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) are introducing new technologies, initiatives, and applications. To assure that these developments do not translate into potential risks that are not captured, understood, measured, and managed, a trustworthiness approach is necessary. AI trustworthiness is treated as a multidimensional construct that spans transparency, safety, security, privacy, robustness, and fairness. We argue that these properties they should be translated into explicit, testable criteria. This article aims to synthesize evaluation approaches that make AI trustworthiness observable and measurable, enabling stakeholders to identify gaps, prioritize improvements, and align system behaviour with ethical, social, and legal values. A scoping review (resulting in 27 papers) is augmented with knowledge of 6 experts to map (i) the main trustworthy AI aspects, (ii) the evaluation methods used to assess these aspects, (iii) the metrics applied within them, and (iv) recommendations proposed to strengthen trustworthiness. The results suggest that current evaluation practices interpret and operationalize trustworthy AI in diverse ways. They often rely on established methods or benchmarks that may imply bias, limited comparability, or provide limited insight into the reasoning quality. We recommend to design evaluation frameworks that explicitly target trustworthiness aspects from a multidisciplinary angle and being instantiated to specific contexts or problems.
items.title: Evaluation methods and metrics towards trustworthy AI
Exploring latent heterogeneity in AI responsibility: a person-centered analysis of ethical dispositions
Informed consent and AI driven depression screening systems

items.abstract: Abstract AI technologies in healthcare are increasingly subject to ethical scrutiny, often structured around high‑level ethical principles such as fairness, transparency, and accountability. While these principles are widely endorsed, their application frequently remains abstract, underspecified, and detached from the empirical contexts in which AI systems are developed and used. This paper argues that empirical ethics provides a necessary foundation for applied AI ethics in healthcare by enabling the ethically relevant contextualisation of normative principles through a reciprocal relationship between empirical and normative ethical analysis. In doing so, the paper addresses a persistent gap between ethical principles and empirical research in AI ethics by showing how these domains can be methodologically integrated rather than treated as separate or sequential. Drawing on empirical examples and our own experience from medical AI research and stakeholder engagement, we illustrate how empirical inquiry and normative ethical analysis, can work together to clarify the meaning of ethical values such as fairness, identify ethically salient risks and trade‑offs, and support ethically robust decision‑making across the AI lifecycle, including research, development, and procurement. We argue that without systematic and methodologically grounded empirical engagement, AI ethics risks becoming either toothless or merely procedural, or sliding into forms of ethical relativism in which empirical findings are treated as normatively sufficient. The article contributes to ongoing debates on how to operationalise AI ethics and highlights the role that empirical ethics can play in bridging ethical theory, law, and practice.
items.title: Why applied AI ethics in healthcare requires the integration of empirical inquiry and normative ethical analysis

items.abstract: Abstract Our study investigates the inter-dependencies between the technical components of AI-based fraud detection systems and fairness approaches. Here, fairness approaches refer to any method or process to address, specify, measure or mitigate unfairness in AI systems. Despite extensive research on both AI-based fraud detection systems and AI fairness, these domains are often treated separately, leading to a fragmented understanding of both domains. This fragmentation leads to inconsistent terminologies and concepts, and fails to identify the inter-dependencies between technical components of fraud detection systems and fairness approaches. These are the research gaps we address in this study. Through a literature review of 78 papers, we synthesize existing concepts and terminologies into two structured taxonomies that allow to document these inter-dependencies. One taxonomy describes the technical components of AI fraud detection systems and another describes fairness approaches. A joint evaluation of the taxonomies reveals how technical components are impacting fairness, and how fairness considerations should govern the design and implementation of these technical components. Our findings show that four technical components (regarding class imbalance, overlapping class distributions, data quality, and adaptive learning) are intertwined with fairness approaches in fraud detection. The proposed taxonomies, and the inter-dependencies we identify, support AI practitioners and decision-makers in designing fair fraud detection systems. Additionally, the taxonomies provide structure to research investigating how technical components and technical decisions impact fairness and, vice versa, investigating how fairness approaches impact the technical design of fraud detection systems.
items.title: Taxonomies for connecting technical components of AI-based fraud detection systems and fairness approaches

items.abstract: Abstract AI-text detectors are increasingly used to police authorship in student assessment and scholarly publishing. This paper argues that they are the wrong instrument for that task. Its design combines a critical synthesis of empirical, information-theoretic, and policy evidence with an original documented exploratory multi-tool audit. The review synthesises empirical evaluations, information-theoretic results, and institutional policy decisions to develop a conceptual account of what detectors can directly observe: statistical or learned properties of submitted text, not provenance itself. Predictability-related properties such as low perplexity, reduced variation in local predictability, and formulaic density provide one mechanism through which both additional-language writing and highly conventional academic prose may become vulnerable to machine-authorship classification. While a growing number of universities across several national higher-education systems have disabled or restricted AI detection in high-stakes assessment, and a New York court has annulled a misconduct finding that rested on a detector score, detector reliance persists in three under-examined arenas: individual grading practice at scale, scholarly journal screening, and institutions without formal policy revision. The paper adds a documented exploratory multi-tool audit in which a single human-authored manuscript, submitted to five commercial detectors on the same day, received materially different classifications spanning from “0% human” to “Human Generated”, demonstrating substantial cross-tool inconsistency and limited independent verifiability of the underlying classifications. A paired exploratory comparison further found that extensive machine rewriting by a commercial “humanizer” materially degraded the manuscript while producing only a small change in the reported detection score. The paper distinguishes genuine false positives from definitional boundary cases involving AI-assisted translation and polishing, engages the counter-argument that AI-polished prose may itself flatten linguistic diversity in academic English, and proposes a concrete process-oriented assessment model based on declared starting points, versioned drafting, process artefacts, and targeted oral verification. The model predates generative AI in its component practices but acquires renewed relevance because final-text classification cannot establish authorship, understanding, or misconduct on its own.
items.title: The pitfalls of AI detection in academic writing: bias, false positives, and the need for inclusive assessment

items.abstract: Abstract Efforts to promote “Trustworthy AI” have focused on operationalizing high-level ethical principles through tools, standards, and governance mechanisms. Yet a persistent gap remains between ethical guidance and day-to-day development practice. We conducted semi-structured interviews with ten experts in AI ethics, healthcare AI, and socio-technical research to examine how ethical principles are operationalized in real-world AI development. Participants described several ways in which efforts to operationalize ethical principles break down in practice. While existing operationalization approaches were viewed as useful, participants discussed conceptual, epistemic, institutional, and socio-technical conditions that constrain their effectiveness. Our findings suggest that the operationalization gap cannot be understood independently of the broader contexts in which AI systems are designed, developed, and governed.
items.title: How ethics operationalization breaks down in practice: expert perspectives from healthcare AI
A dilemma for skeptics of trustworthy AI
Generative AI in peer review: evolving policies and regulatory pathways for scientific rigour
Compiling governance into enforcement: risk-tiered, confidence-aware fairness gates for machine-learning pipelines

items.abstract: Abstract Epistemic injustice happens when a subject is wronged in their “capacity as a knower.” This paper argues that speakers/writers and hearers/readers suffer epistemic injustice under two scenarios: idea appropriation and bullshitting. Epistemic injustice happens when a speaker or writer suffers idea appropriation, where they are deprived of the credit and benefits of their cognitive labor, or when epistemic agents consume bullshit that exploits their limited access to the institutional resources required to interrogate and resist it, treating them as a mere means to an end, e.g., when a politician bullshits voters to secure their vote at election time. These unsavory practices are incentivized by reputational boosts and other social goods with the risk of reputational damage if detected. This paper ends by reviewing how widespread epistemic injustice hampers the epistemic marketplace.
items.title: Unjust Aspects of the Epistemic Marketplace: Idea Appropriation, Bullshit, and Epistemic Injustice

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines the work of legal intermediaries in moving cases from the border to the court, focusing on pushbacks from Italy and Austria to Slovenia and along the Balkan corridor. It demonstrates that these practices occurred within a hostile transnational setting that, from the outset, dispersed and destabilized potential claimants, traces, and the litigation path. Confronted with this immediate condition of misalignment, it shows that intermediaries engaged in constitutive and collaborative work across borders. The article conceptualizes this work as “case assembly” and analyzes it from a comparative perspective.
items.title: From borders to courts: assembling pushback cases in a hostile transnational setting

items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents Paul Roth’s Paradox of Historical Narratives and three options: reject the paradox, accept the paradox, or resolve the paradox. I show how the paradox motivates a view called ‘narrativism’ in the philosophy of history, and that narrativists must either accept or resolve the paradox. I argue that narrativists should resolve the paradox.
items.title: Revisiting Roth’s Paradox of Historical Narratives

items.abstract: Abstract Generative AI threatens knowledge online not merely by producing falsehoods, but by changing the epistemic environment in which online beliefs are formed. I argue that the spread of convincing AI-generated counterfeits creates a local sceptical challenge to digital testimony. The challenge is not that ordinary subjects must rule out every sceptical possibility. Rather, for many beliefs formed solely from unauthenticated online materials, ordinary subjects are situated among nearby, method-indistinguishable bad cases. In such environments, even true beliefs formed from genuine digital items may fail to satisfy a familiar anti-luck condition on knowledge. This does not show that we never know from online sources. It shows instead that digital-only uptake often falls short of knowledge unless supported by provenance, corroboration, or other independent checks. I close by suggesting that this narrowing of online knowledge may reinforce existing patterns of epistemic injustice.
items.title: Generative AI and a Sceptical Challenge to Digital Testimony

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines contemporary digital governance through a dialogue between Shoshana Zuboff's theory of surveillance capitalism and Michel Foucault's analysis of power and governmentality. Although Zuboff offers a compelling account of the economic logics underlying digital domination, her framework tends to locate resistance primarily in external regulation and legal reform. This article argues that such an approach overlooks the subjectifying effects through which digital governance shapes compliant and predictable subjects. Drawing on Foucault, it reconceptualizes surveillance capitalism as an intensification of existing governmental rationalities and advances the notion of counter‐conduct to analyze how subjects negotiate and resist digital power from within.
items.title: Surveillance Capitalism and Governmentality Foucault in the Age of Digitization

items.abstract: ABSTRACT According to veritism, your epistemic goal is to believe what's true. According to actualist veritism, your epistemic goal is to believe what's actually true. At first glance, it seems that the pursuit of truth and the pursuit of actual truth will lead to the same destination. This will follow for evidential decision theorists; but if we are causal decision theorists (as I am), then pursuing truth and pursuing actual truth will lead us to different destinations. In this paper, I assume causal decision theory and argue for actualist veritism over veritism. My argument is that veritism does not respect the direction of fit of belief, since it incentivizes changing the world to match your beliefs, rather than changing your beliefs to match the world as it is. In contrast, actualist veritism honors the direction of fit of belief, and only incentivizes changing your beliefs to match the world as it is. For this reason, actualist veritism allows epistemic teleologists to escape “epistemic bribery” objections, to doubt self‐verifying propositions like “someone believes this proposition,” and to maintain coherence in the face of self‐falsifying propositions like “I don't believe this proposition.”
items.title: Epistemic Actualism

items.abstract: Human infection challenge (HIC) studies where healthy volunteers are deliberately infected expedite vaccine development. However, agreement on fair compensation that avoids both exploitation and undue inducement remains elusive. Without clear compensation policies or guidelines, implementation of HIC studies remains a challenge in Zambia. We conducted 5 focus group discussions and 15 in-depth interviews on compensation prior to initiation of a typhoid HIC study among healthy adults from higher learning institutions in Lusaka, Zambia. Thematic analysis revealed HIC-specific considerations for compensation, including compensation allocated to research participants and their families for potential risk of immediate and long-term side effects from deliberate infection. Preferences for compensation timing varied, with some advocating for upfront compensation and others favouring compensation after participation to account for lived experiences of side-effects, time commitment and emotional burden. Compensation preferences included monetary and non-monetary compensation in the form of long-term medical coverage and tuition for university/college education. However, views on the value of the compensation varied, highlighting the complexity of determining appropriate compensation that balances voluntariness with fair recognition of risks and sacrifices. Sustained engagement of ethics and regulatory authorities with potential research participants must be encouraged to ensure ethically responsive research and to build public trust in HIC studies.
items.title: “This is human life, so I don’t know what compensation I can attach to it”: perceptions on compensation in human infection challenge studies in Lusaka, Zambia
Ethical implications of the mereology of pregnancy: a response to commentaries
Humanitarianism or toxic colonialism? The burdens of unusable drug donations during crises

items.abstract: Recent philosophers of secularization have given religion a more central place in their thinking about secular modernity and liberal democracy. This article argues that such theories have overlooked an important dimension of the contemporary social and political landscape, namely how the framework of separating ‘religious’ and ‘secular’ spheres can paradoxically affirm the hegemonic position of Christianity and marginalize non-Christian minorities. Drawing on the work of Gil Anidjar, the article instead develops a critical narrative of secularization which points to continuations of Christian hegemony in the ‘secular’ realm, despite and through the religion-secular binary. Bringing this to the forefront is crucial for understanding how secularism can be compatible with the rise in Christian nationalist politics in Europe and North America, as well as the marginalization of racial and religious minorities. Moreover, the article argues, rethinking secularization raises important new questions for normative theory about religion and politics.
items.title: Rethinking Secularization: The Religion-Secular Binary, Christianity, and the Politics of Exclusion
From Sacred Spaces to the Workplace: How Religious Third-Place Participation Fosters Helping Behaviors Through Awe-Based Spillover

items.abstract: Abstract Despite business ethics drawing on a wide range of philosophical perspectives, conservative thought remains strikingly underrepresented in the field. This paper addresses that absence by bringing the conservative philosophical tradition into conversation with business ethics. It first provides an overview of conservative thought, focussing in particular on Burke, Oakeshott, and Scruton. It then examines three strands of business ethics scholarship that appear to have affinities with conservative thought, namely libertarianism, the market failures approach, and virtue ethics, in order to identify possible points of dialogue with existing debates. Finally, the paper outlines a research agenda for conservative business ethics, highlighting issues such as conservative critiques of capitalism, environmental sustainability, and family business.
items.title: Whither Conservative Business Ethics? Addressing the Puzzling Absence of Conservative Thought in Business Ethics
Gender Is Essential to Some, But Not All, Individuals

items.abstract: This study assesses the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on Indian economy. To do so, we first analyse the linkage between AI, employment and economic growth. Second, this study elaborates on the role of AI in shaping India’s Human Development Index (HDI) and compares it with three major economies. Finally, to supplement the analysis, the article makes a quantitative assessment of the effect of AI on economic growth in India. The analysis does not reveal that the displacement effect of AI on employment outweighs the complementary effect in the Indian context so far. However, from the demand side perspective, there might be a reduction in demand for non-AI-related jobs and an increase in AI-related jobs. Further, results show that an increase in AI vibrancy index support better performance of HDI in India in comparison to the China, Germany and the US. Finally, by employing an ARDL model, the results reveal that AI only positively affect the economic growth in the long-run but not in the short run. From a policy perspective, while the Government of India has taken proactive steps for AI-enabled schemes, greater emphasis on appropriate strategies is required to generate more employment through the adoption of AI.
items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Indian Economy: Prospects and Challenges

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and Industry 4.0 technologies are transforming manufacturing systems globally, with significant implications for labour markets in emerging economies. This article examines how AI adoption reshapes employment structures, skills demand, and training effectiveness in the automotive manufacturing sector in Vietnam. Drawing on the frameworks of skill-biased technological change and routine-biased technological change, the study develops an integrated model linking AI adoption to task reconfiguration, skills mismatch, and employment outcomes. Using labour force statistics, the findings show that AI adoption increases demand for high-skilled and hybrid technical workers while reducing demand for others. However, substantial skills mismatches persist, particularly among domestic firms and small and medium-sized enterprises. Training systems play a critical mediating role, with firms investing in workforce development experiencing better productivity and labour retention outcomes. The article argues that, without coordinated policies linking industrial upgrading, skills development, and social protection, AI-driven transformation may exacerbate inequality.
items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Skills Mismatch and Inclusive Industrial Transformation: Evidence from Vietnam’s Automotive Sector

items.abstract: This article introduces the concept of state culture to describe the subtle but profound ways in which the modern state shapes norms, values, language, and social conventions. Although property rights and formal freedoms may persist, cultural life is increasingly influenced—if not dominated—by state interventions. Through education, media control, financial incentives, and regulation, the state fosters a cultural environment that supports its own legitimacy and expansion. This has given rise to phenomena such as wokeness, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) compliance, and cancel culture, which are not spontaneous expressions of civil society but symptoms of a long-standing cultural distortion induced by state power. Many seemingly private decisions—such as corporate censorship and social ostracism—occur within this distorted cultural framework and cannot be interpreted as fully voluntary. As such, libertarians face a dilemma: While they must defend property rights, they must also recognize that culture itself can be corrupted through systematic violations of property rights. Drawing on insights from Murray Rothbard, the article proposes that state institutions, as long as they exist, should be operated in ways that align with the cultural norms that would emerge in a truly free society. The goal is not cultural neutrality—impossible under statism—but the active support of values conducive to liberty: private property, personal responsibility, truth, family, and voluntary cooperation.
items.title: The Problem of State Culture

items.abstract: The main aspiration of the present article is to elucidate what it would mean for the paradox of blackmail to be solved rather than dissolved . We begin by increasing the sense of paradoxicality of blackmail. To this end, we formalize the paradox. We demonstrate that it relies on a certain prima facie plausible principle of closure (what we call disjunctive closure ). This principle is quite unlike the principle which holds that the permissibility of action A and the permissibility of action B render doing A and B together permissible. On the principle of disjunctive closure, the paradox of blackmail seems to breed a genuine contradiction. Having adequately formulated the paradox, we turn to a normative point: What would count as a satisfactory solution to the paradox of blackmail? Informed by the treatment of paradoxes in logic, we argue that to take the sting out of the paradox of blackmail, we must embrace its core commitments and still explain how apparently contradictory verdicts might nevertheless arise. The upshot of the above considerations only strengthens our contention that what we proposed as a solution to the paradox of blackmail in Dominiak and Wysocki (2026) is indeed an adequate solution rather than a mere dissolution .
items.title: How Is the Paradox of Blackmail Paradoxical?

items.abstract: Abstract The legal field already uses various large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications. The practical use in the patent domain concentrates on general pre-trained and foundation models without domain specificity. However, little is known and documented about their performance; their limitations are poorly studied and documented. Quality control and any targeted improvement of natural language processing in patent law require such information. We evaluated several open-source and proprietary LLMs—including the GPT series, Anthropic, DeepSeek, and Llama-3 variants—on parts of the European qualifying examination (EQE) for future European patent attorneys. The chosen tests are intentionally technical and designed with little room for interpretation so that models cannot hide wrong associations and answers behind apparent eloquence. OpenAI o1 led with 0.82 accuracy and 0.81 F1 score, whereas AWS (Amazon Web Services) Llama 3.1 8B lagged at 0.50 accuracy, and a Python-deployed Llama 3.1 8B scored 0.55. The latter two are within the range of mere guessing for the two-option forced-choice design. None of the evaluated models could have fully passed the examination, as accuracy never exceeded the average threshold of 0.90 required for professional-level standards—also not models that are regularly promoted for their assumed beyond-PhD- and bar-admitted-lawyer-level performance. GPT-4o excelled at integrating text and graphics, whereas Claude 3 Opus often struggled to maintain formatting coherence. Human patent experts evaluated the textual justifications to identify and understand problems at the argument level. They uncovered various critical shortcomings of each model. They valued clarity and legal rationale over the raw correctness of the answers, which revealed misalignment between automatic metrics and expert judgment. Model outputs were sensitive to modest temperature changes and prompt wording, which underscores the continued necessity of expert oversight. Although the arguments and our analysis of the training corpora demonstrate that the relevant legal texts were part of pre-training, the models, e.g., their embeddings, demonstrated potential for improvement in domain-specific language aspects. Future work should target logical consistency, robust multimodality, and adaptive prompting to approach human-level patent proficiency. In summary, despite the outstanding performance of recent large models, the general public might overestimate their capabilities. The field has a long way to go to develop a virtual patent attorney. This paper aims to point out several specific limitations that need solutions.
items.title: Can general large language models (LLM) pass a hands-on patent attorney test? A study on LLM capabilities
Equality in Practice: How Country-Level Leave Entitlements Shape Women’s Career Development Opportunities in Organizations

items.abstract: Abstract This study examined how companies visually constructed intersectional gender representation in their social media posts and how Generative AI may reproduce or reshape these practices. Drawing on gender representation research in corporate communication, the Stereotype Content Model, and visual social semiotics, we analyzed 300 Instagram posts from the top 100 Fortune 500 B2C companies alongside 300 AI-generated images created to mirror them. Using mixed-methods visual social semiotic content analysis, we compared compositional, interactional, and representational meanings, positioning representation as distributive and recognitional justice. Findings indicated that corporate imagery often signaled performative inclusivity in compositional and interactional meanings, while reinforcing persistent hierarchies in representational meanings. In contrast, AI-generated imagery appeared anamorphic, sometimes reflecting dominant representational patterns and other times distorting or reversing them in ways that rendered identity markers ambiguous or exaggerated. These findings highlight ethical challenges in integrating AI into corporate communication and underscore the need for organizational reflexivity, transparency, and accountability in visual content creation. This study contributes to emerging scholarship on AI ethics and gender representation in corporate communication and offers practical guidance for managers seeking to ensure that the use of AI supports inclusivity and social justice.
items.title: Intersectional Gender Representation in Corporate Social Media and Corresponding AI-Generated Images: Hallucinatory AI or Anamorphic AI in a House of Illusions?

items.abstract: Abstract It is one of the most frequent criticisms of regularity theories of causation that they cannot distinguish between causes and effects based on Boolean determination relations of sufficiency and necessity alone—jeopardizing their goal of reducing causation to Boolean determination. The criticism rests on the fact that determination relations can be symmetric but causation (in acyclic structures) cannot. Regularity theorists have countered by arguing that only simplistic determination structures are symmetric, and by insisting that structures with a minimal complexity of two alternative causes per effect exhibit non-symmetric determination relations. In this paper, we show that this regularity-theoretic response is insufficient to break symmetries of determination and, thus, to identify the direction of causation. To solve this problem, we introduce a new directionality criterion and demonstrate that it suffices to distinguish causes from effects solely on the basis of Boolean determination relations.
items.title: Breaking Symmetry: A New Directionality Criterion for Regularity Theories of Causation

items.abstract: Abstract This essay examines the theoretical relation between moral sentiments and the goodness of human nature in Mengzi's moral philosophy. Mengzi's claim that human nature is good is often understood through the heart of compassion and the sages' exemplary achievements. I argue that both approaches are incomplete: they show how the moral potential is actualized but insufficiently explains how the goodness of human nature itself is recognized or validated. Instead, I argue that Mengzi also suggests a spectatorial account of moral evaluation. From the spectator's standpoint, we discern goodness through shared sentiments of approbation, which are grounded in the hearts of shame and approval. Our approvals of virtuous agents function to indicate their goodness and provide empirical support for the claim that human nature contains an inherent potential for goodness. I show the merit of this spectatorial perspective with an enriched interpretation of 3A1, where the claim that human nature is good first appears. By combining agential and spectatorial perspectives, Mengzi develops a coherent account of the goodness of human nature that encourages agential moral self‐cultivation, strengthened from a spectatorial examination of goodness.
items.title: Why Does Mengzi Consider Human Nature Good?

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Referential indeterminacy may seem to leave little room for de re or singular thoughts about ordinary objects. I argue that this impression is misleading. We can direct our thoughts at particular objects, even though there is no fact of the matter as to which objects are referred to by the singular terms purporting to stand for them. By distinguishing between weak and strong de re attitudes, I show that speakers can retain a weak form of de re belief despite the absence of determinate reference. I extend the same distinction to knowledge of reference, thereby explaining how linguistic understanding survives the indeterminacy of reference. I also briefly explore some broader implications of this picture for the theory of reference and for the status of genuine singular terms.
items.title:
Referential Indeterminacy and
                    De Re
                    Thoughts

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines the ethical and legal dimensions of corporate land grabbing in Bahia, Brazil, focusing on the forestry sector’s use of fraud, legal manipulation, and violence to acquire land. Through a case study of Veracel Celulose, a joint venture between the Swedish-Finnish corporation Stora Enso and the Brazilian company Suzano, we analyze how corporations exploit legal ambiguity and manipulate land registries to dispossess local populations. Drawing on archival data from federal and state land governance institutions, we develop the concept of corporate (il)legal enclosure, defined as the process through which corporations transform contested, public, or informally held land into de facto corporate property by mobilizing intertwined legal and illegal practices that exclude local populations from access, use, and control over land. Our findings show how title forgery, cadastral manipulation, administrative procedures, and legal regularization operate together to convert fraudulent land claims into seemingly legitimate corporate property. We demonstrate that land grabbing increasingly occurs not only through violence or outright illegality, but through the strategic mobilization of legal and bureaucratic institutions that render dispossession lawful in practice. By integrating insights from agrarian studies, sociolegal scholarship, and business ethics, the article advances a contextually grounded understanding of land-based injustice and challenges compliance-oriented approaches to business ethics. In doing so, it highlights the need for business ethics scholarship to engage more directly with the role of law in enabling and legitimizing corporate dispossession.
items.title: Corporate (Il)legal Enclosures: How Fraudulent Land Titles Override Community Rights in Forestry Land Conflicts in Bahia, Brazil
Werner Stegmaier, What is Orientation? A Philosophical Investigation. (Transl. by Reinhard G. Mueller) Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter, 2019, 298 pp. $ 36 (Pbk)

items.abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the semantic properties of memory reports in the Iranian languages Persian and Sorani Kurdish. In these languages, memory predicates are constructed out of a noun meaning ‘memory,’ the copula, and a locative preposition. I demonstrate that memory predicates in these languages pass diagnostics for abstract state predicates, distinguishing them from imagination reports, to which memory reports have been compared in the recent philosophical and linguistic literature. Building on decompositional approaches to attitude predicates, I develop a novel compositional semantics for memory predicates in these languages that accounts for their form, stativity, and differences from imagination predicates. This work contributes to the growing literature on the semantics of memory reports in natural language cross-linguistically, and discusses implications for the relationship between natural language semantics and the philosophy of memory.
items.title: Memory reports as state descriptions: an Iranian perspective
Beyond Sovereign Recognition: Structural Harm and the Foundations of Peremptory Norms
The Idea of Progress: Critical Perspectives
The alignment problem is an illusion

items.abstract: Abstract Recently, watermarking schemes for large language models (LLMs) have been proposed to distinguish between text generated by machines and by humans. This paper explores philosophical, political, and ethical ramifications of developing and deploying watermarking schemes. A definition of authorship attribution that encompasses both machines (LLMs) and humans is proposed as a backdrop. It is argued that private watermarks may provide private companies with sweeping rights to determine authorship, which is incompatible with traditional standards of authorship attribution. Then, possible ramifications of the so-called “entropy dependence” of watermarking mechanisms are explored. It is argued that entropy levels may vary across different, socially salient groups. This could lead to group-dependent disparities in the detection rates of machine-generated text. Specifically, groups with a greater interest in low-entropy text may face challenges in detecting machine-generated text that is of interest to them.
items.title: The ramifications of LLM watermarks for authorship and groups
Artificial intelligence, judicial precedent and responsible judicial AI governance in Uganda: ethical, constitutional and institutional implications of AI-assisted legal research

items.abstract: Abstract We consider the application of automated machine learning models in a real credit lending platform, and empirically study whether the trade-off between fairness and profitability can be improved by means of fairness processing methods. Fairness is evaluated along the principle of Separation, while profitability is computed as a loan-level profit function, aggregated at the portfolio level. The empirical findings reveal that none of the considered fairness processors reduces bias without an increase in costs, in the form of higher false positive or of higher false negative rates.
items.title: Fairness versus profitability in automated machine learning

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates communication, interpretation, decision-making, and knowledge production, raising questions about how computational systems acquire epistemic authority. At the same time, resistance to AI is emerging across educational, creative, infrastructural, professional, and civic settings. This conceptual paper examines what such resistance reveals about the distribution and contestability of epistemic authority in AI-mediated environments. Drawing on Science and Technology Studies, critical AI studies, AI ethics, political philosophy, and epistemic theory, it extends emerging accounts of AI-mediated epistemic capture by connecting them to epistemic agency, resistance, and governance . Epistemic capture is conceptualized as a gradual and relational process through which interpretive authority can become increasingly organized around computational systems and difficult to contest. The paper develops a typology encompassing quiet refusal, epistemic, infrastructural, educational, creative, and decolonial resistance, together with reclamation, while emphasizing that resistance is not inherently emancipatory or epistemically beneficial. Instead, resistance can operate diagnostically by revealing conditions under which epistemic agency becomes constrained. Building on this argument, the paper develops a relational epistemic governance framework integrating reflexivity, transparency, contestability, human adjudication, epistemic pluralism, democratic legitimacy, and sustainability. The framework shifts attention from governing AI systems alone toward the institutional organization of epistemic authority: who can interpret, challenge, adjudicate, and reshape AI-mediated knowledge, and under what conditions such authority remains democratically accountable.
items.title: AI resistance and epistemic agency: toward a relational framework for democratic and human-centered AI governance
Developing nonviolent artificial intelligence: nonviolence as a principle of ethical AI
From principlism to practice: a five-principle safeguard framework for workplace AI

items.abstract: Abstract This article makes a case for creative methods in legal research that is both analytical and moral. Beginning with an information-theoretical account of legal evolution, I propose a shift from ‘law as language’ and ‘law as communication’ to the more foundational unit of information coded by legal language. I conceptually clarify ‘legal coding’ as the process by which legal meanings get constructed and conceptualised, and position the legal academy as an active site of legal coding. Critically examining the information that is excluded from legal codes (because of ignorance, irrelevance, or illegibility) opens pathways to reveal, challenge, and shift the selective and patterned tendencies of legal coding processes to reinforce epistemic injustice. Positioning the legal academy as a site of legal coding further helps in understanding legal research as a practice of legal coding. I argue that expanding our methodological toolkits can enable a more holistic coding of social reality. By expanding the form of legal codes, creative methods equip us to capture new (or previously excluded) information about lived realities that remain on the margins of meanings. The analytical case for coding social reality more holistically, by including new forms of information through a creative praxis, is complemented by a moral case to include alternative perspectives and hermeneutically misunderstood lives. I demonstrate these arguments through a self-produced short film ‘(IN)VISIBLE’ that captures the working lives of Indian women legal experts, towards a grounded theory of legal evolution from the south. The film combines embodied, poetic, sonic, and visual analyses to capture and analyse legal coding from the point of view of my research participants. My discussions on the process and output of the film show how a phenomenological analysis can help reveal the structural, allowing for a more complete and just coding of social reality, from within the academy.
items.title: Towards epistemic justice: a case for creative methods in legal research

items.abstract: Abstract Russia’s war in Ukraine has revived the European Union’s enlargement policy, placing it at the forefront of the EU’s priorities. This process is being viewed as the next phase of EU enlargement, encompassing the Western Balkans, Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia. This article examines the new framework for EU accession negotiations adopted in 2022, which regrouped the chapters of the acquis (presently 35 negotiating chapters) into six clusters.
