The article presents a case study on the Western Balkans, highlighting both their achievements and shortcomings in strengthening the rule of law and how the new framework is being applied to them. It analyses whether the EU has expanded the rule of law conditionality across the negotiating chapters in the new clusters format as a pre-emptive measure regarding EU candidate states’ ability to uphold the rule of law and their commitments to fundamental rights before joining the Union. Furthermore, it assesses whether the reform of the EU accession negotiations framework has been influenced by the experience of rule of law erosion and backsliding in Poland and Hungary, as well as assessing the reasons for including some EU candidate states from the Western Balkans in the annual Rule of Law Report mechanism while conditioning EU funds on their respect for the rule of law.
items.title: The rule of law in EU enlargement policy

items.abstract: Abstract Anticipated with interest and unease, the Grand Chamber of the Court of Justice delivered its judgment on the Adequate Minimum Wages Directive 2022/2041/EU in November 2025. Although it annulled limited criteria on setting and updating statutory minimum wages, the Directive was upheld, including its legal basis in Article 153(1)(b) TFEU. The Court thereby accommodated divergent wage-setting systems embedding the Directive within the social objectives of Title X TFEU, and finding that Art. 153(5) limits EU action only where a measure concretely amounts to direct interference. Both elements contrast sharply with the Opinion of Advocate General Emiliou, which proposed a broad reading of the pay exclusion to annul the Directive. This careful judgment is a landmark in labour law and EU law. Far beyond a decision on competence exclusions, it positively develops a space for an exercise of EU competence that preserves the capacity to realise Social Europe’s objectives; respects social partner autonomy and Member State diversity, and promotes collective bargaining. In the article, we characterise these three dimensions as the judgment’s somewhat hidden theory of Social Europe. This theory can sharpen arguments for advancing Social Europe, articulating its levels and actors, and pursuing upward social convergence. It clarifies the constitutional position and working methods of the social policy title, allows its developments and limits to be evaluated, and enables anticipation of how and why Social Europe initiatives may succeed or fail. More than the endpoint of an annulment challenge, the judgment and its theory are resources whose advances and limits are to be mined.
items.title: Beyond competence exclusions: the hidden theory of Social Europe in the judgement on the Adequate Minimum Wages Directive

items.abstract: Abstract After COVID-19 and the Russian invasion of Ukraine, many countries levied windfall taxes on specific sectors that obtained abnormal levels of profitability (e.g. banking, energy, food distribution). Windfall taxation is evolving from the traditional taxing of unearned profit due to luck (i.e. extraordinary profit due to interest rate rise) to taxing profits derived from unsustainable practices (i.e. profit-shifting in Pillar Two). Such a shift reveals the profound crisis of corporate income tax on tax business profit and places windfall taxation as an interim solution to collect tax revenue. This need to collect revenue complicates and renders incoherent the legal design of windfall taxes (in-scope rules, taxable base and tax rate) under the ability to pay and equality principle. To prevent creating a tax on general income, the legislator struggles to single out the industries subject to the tax, calculate the taxable base (extraordinary profit) and determine a tax rate. Such tensions reveal the difficulties of drawing lines in taxing business profits and suggest the need for a fully fledged reform of corporate taxation.
items.title: The evolving nature of windfall taxation: an interim measure for a broken corporate tax?

items.abstract: Abstract This Article reinterprets the Apple State aid case through a Transformative Law and Political Economy (TLPE) lens. It argues that the Court of Justice’s 2024 judgment showed that, under specific national-law conditions, State aid control can reach aggressive tax planning by prioritizing economic substance over formal profit allocation. Apple thus marked the high-water point of the Commission’s post-2013 effort to use Article 107 TFEU as a meso–level governance tool linking firm-specific tax rulings to broader distortions in the internal market. At the same time, the case exposed the limits of this strategy. Parallel enforcement actions failed, and subsequent legislative initiatives encountered comparable resistance rooted in sovereignty claims, unanimity requirements, evidentiary asymmetries, and geopolitical constraints. Read through a TLPE lens, the Apple saga reveals both the contingent possibilities and the structural limits of EU legal strategies to constrain corporate tax avoidance. While law can expose the contingency of entrenched arrangements, durable institutional redesign ultimately depends on political-economic conditions that legal intervention alone cannot generate.
items.title: Not Rotten, Not Bad: Rethinking Apple and EU Tax Governance through Law and Political Economy

items.abstract: Abstract Embodiment is a particularly difficult dimension of experience to capture for transgender individuals, particularly individuals who identify as nonbinary. Accounts of embodiment in both philosophy and psychology often fail to capture the layers of perplexity which nonbinary individuals experience when attempting to understand the relationship between the lived body and social perceptions of the body. In reading Merleau-Ponty’s late work in The visible and the invisible , particularly the much-discussed notion of the chiasm, I attempt to work toward a potential remedy for phenomenology’s difficulty accounting for this particular dimension of experience. Drawing extensively on Megan Burke’s (2022) discussion of the notion of cis sense, I elaborate the implications of the ontological principle of the chiasm in relation to the nonbinary experience of the body. Through a close reading of the implications of Merleau-Ponty’s particular understanding of “invisibility,” I conclude that the application of the ontological principle of the chiasm to the nonbinary experience of the body is fruitful conceptually, as it offers a powerful language through which to counter normative and reifying ways of accounting for the body. Ultimately, a chiasmatic account presents a dynamic body which emerges from preeminent first-person authority over embodiment.
items.title: Crossing the Chiasm: Queering the Ontology of the Chiasm in Merleau-Ponty’s Phenomenology

items.abstract: Abstract Thomas Paine is widely known for galvanizing public opinion in favor of the cause of American independence; his trenchant critique of Edmund Burke and spirited affirmation of the “rights of man”; and his contribution to the development of republicanism during constitutional debates in France. Yet there has been less scholarly attention to what is arguably Paine’s greatest revolution: namely, his vision of the United States as a “civic nation” whose membership is determined by consent to shared republican principles. A closer examination of Paine’s life and political writings reveals the strengths as well as the weaknesses of this civic ideal.
items.title: Thomas Paine’s Greatest Revolution: Nationality, Citizenship, and Civic Identity in America

items.abstract: Abstract This article extends Eric Voegelin’s analysis of symbolic forms to modern constitutionalism. Voegelin viewed symbols not merely as functional or superficially representative, but as articulations of reality. Therefore, this article proposes “permeability” as a core diagnostic concept. It constructs a novel symbolic framework for secular politics that establishes a creative tension between foundational “ontological human rights” and specific “practical human rights.” This article explores Voegelin’s concept of “reflective distance” to outline a potential method for analyzing the coherence between constitutional symbols and the state of national consciousness. It thereby lays the philosophical groundwork for assessing a symbolic framework’s health.
items.title: Symbolization of Constitutionalism: A Voegelinian Approach

items.abstract: Abstract We consider axioms under which population principles face an unavoidable choice between accepting the Repugnant Conclusion or the Very Sadistic Conclusion. Our analysis reveals that this dilemma persists even without imposing the axiom of Anonymity. This significantly broadens the ethical implications when considering populations that differ in temporal, spatial or probabilistic dimensions or when including non-human populations. Imposing Existence Independence, combined with an Archimedean axiom that we term the Strict Limit Property, is sufficient for the dilemma to arise. These findings substantially generalize previous impossibility results in population ethics and highlight the inescapable trade-offs faced by any coherent population principle.
items.title: The dilemma between repugnancy and sadism extends beyond critical-level utilitarianism

items.abstract: Abstract This paper argues that the standard rationale for regulating markets also applies to democracy. Economists and philosophers commonly defend government intervention in markets on the grounds that markets predictably suffer from failures such as public goods problems, information asymmetries, principal–agent dilemmas, lack of competition, irrationality, and externalities. Democratic politics exhibits the same failures – often more severely – yet is typically assumed to be exempt from regulation. We challenge this asymmetry by showing that the justificatory structure for market regulation straightforwardly extends to democratic processes. We sketch a range of equality-preserving interventions – such as participation incentives, disclosure and promise-tracking mechanisms, transparent ballot design, and safeguards against catastrophic risks – that regulate democracy without abolishing it. Just as regulating markets is not the same as abolishing them, regulating democratic processes is not undemocratic. Recognizing this parity reframes debates about institutional design and opens a new research agenda in democratic theory.
items.title: Against laissez-faire democracy

items.abstract: Abstract This paper studies Nozick’s invisible-hand account of the minimal state through an extension of Bruner’s model, taking seriously Nozick’s remarks on division of labour and market pressures. I develop a game-theoretic model in which a compatibility premium – higher cooperative success among agents who share protective procedures – transforms part of Nozick’s state of nature into an assurance environment with tipping dynamics. Under suitable parameter values, the model yields a dominant protective agency while preserving side constraints and non-worsening for independents. Commercial compatibility can make Nozick’s invisible-hand story more dynamically plausible, even though the remaining obstacle is coordination rather than conflict alone.
items.title: Division of labour and the minimal state

items.abstract: Abstract Climate impacts extend beyond physical destruction to include widespread financial distress. This article explores the role that debt relief policies – particularly personal insolvency or bankruptcy law – might play within a range of measures to raise the capacity of individuals to withstand climate-related shocks. Through the cancellation of unpayable debt, personal insolvency acts as a form of insurance against the unavoidable risks inherent in a volatile and unpredictable economy. Reviewing the links between climate impacts, debt and default, and the inevitable gaps in supports to victims of these impacts, the paper makes a case for personal insolvency as a rules-based system for stabilising chaotic financial distress associated with disasters and crises. As an extraordinary exception to the law’s usual orientation toward upholding past obligations and facilitating market allocations, bankruptcy might represent an internal means of accommodating the disruptions and contradictions with which climate change confronts the legal system.
items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
items.title: Debt relief as climate policy: the role of personal insolvency law
Science miscommunication
Visual metaphors and their epistemic value

items.abstract: Abstract Human enhancement raises a host of important conceptual and moral questions drawn from ethics and metaphysics, social/political theory, and philosophy of medicine. What does it mean to be human? Is it permissible fundamentally to alter our basic humanity? What would that mean? Critics argue, for example, that it is morally permissible to engage in medical therapy to address disease and disability, but not biotechnology to enhance human capacities. Other detractors raise concerns that genetic enhancement would dehumanize persons, involve morally impermissible research, or serve objectionable social/political goals, violating basic human rights or human dignity. Supporters, however, have been known to contend that enhancement may be morally required to level the playing field, given an unequal natural distribution of genetic advantages, physical talents, and cognitive abilities. Others seek to rewire human freedom, biotechnologically engineering “morally improved” human choices or, perhaps, implanting computer chips in the brain, to avoid criminal behavior or international catastrophe. On whose account of morality would enhancements be objectionable or permissible? More generally, which bioethical norms should guide public law on such matters? This number of the Journal of Medicine and Philosophy brings together an international group of scholars from Hong Kong, Macao, Mainland China, the United States, and Texas, to explore critically such concerns regarding forms of human biotechnology, reasons for and objections to pursing various forms of enhancement, and the centrality of such philosophical questions to bioethics and public policy. Together, these authors present a conceptual geography of the possible meanings, creative realities, and likely limits of human bioenhancement.
items.journal: The Journal of Medicine and Philosophy: A Forum for Bioethics and Philosophy of Medicine
items.title: Human Enhancement, Bioethics, and Moral Diversity: An International Philosophical Endeavor

items.abstract: Abstract In the philosophy of emotion, formal objects explain how emotions evaluate their objects and when they are fitting. Admiration presents a person as excellent, while contempt presents them as defective; excellence and defect are typical formal objects of these emotions. Yet, even when we do not know whether someone has the relevant excellence or defect, prestige or stigma attached to their identity or standing may itself elicit emotion. Bringing emotional intentionality into dialogue with social ontology, I argue that some institutionally constituted evaluative properties can also serve as formal objects. The fittingness of such emotions raises two questions: whether the relevant property genuinely obtains and whether, if so, it has the normative standing required for the emotion to be fitting. This framework explains how emotions can be intelligible yet normatively troubling, while distinguishing proper recognition of institutional roles from status-based idolizing deference or stigmatizing denigration.
items.title: Institutional formal objects and two-level fittingness

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Marco Annoni argued in Bioethics that neither the specified principlism of Beauchamp's and Childress's Principles of Biomedical Ethics (PBE) nor the 2022 revision of the International Code of Medical Ethics (ICoME) by the World Medical Association can provide a suitable basis for global bioethics. In response, we first show that Annoni's effort to disqualify PBE's specified principlism as a suitable basis for global bioethics fails, primarily because of its faulty assumptions about the nature, dominance, and authority of PBE's specifications of principles, whether for particular decisional contexts or for particular moralities. We then turn to his attempt to discredit the ICoME as a possible basis for global bioethics because of what he views as its “lack of political legitimacy,” its “undefined moral foundation,” and its “lack of an explicit procedure to solve internal conflicts between its principles.” We present a range of arguments to show that these efforts also fail, leaving both the ICoME and PBE's specified principlism as viable contenders for a suitable basis in global bioethics.
items.title: Suitable Bases for Global Bioethics: A Critical Response to Marco Annoni

items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is an emerging development in the digital transformation of healthcare. Unlike conventional generative AI, agentic AI systems can perform autonomous, goal-directed actions and coordinate complex tasks. They promise to support or even collaborate with clinicians and patients in increasingly independent ways. While agentic AI raises familiar moral concerns regarding safety, accountability and bias, this article focuses on a less explored dimension: its capacity to transform the moral fabric of healthcare itself. Drawing on the framework of techno-moral change and the three domains of decision, relation and perception, we investigate how agentic AI might reshape the patient–physician relationship and reconfigure core concepts of medical morality. We argue that these shifts, while not fully predictable, demand ethical attention before widespread deployment. Ultimately, the paper calls for integrating ethical foresight into the design and use of agentic AI.
items.title: Agentic AI, medical morality and the transformation of the patient–physician relationship

items.abstract: Arthur Schopenhauer’s philosophy has been systematically excluded from the canon of radical political thought, dismissed as quietist resignation incompatible with emancipatory projects. This article challenges that exclusion by developing the concept of the pluriversal subject, a political subjectivity derived from Schopenhauer’s metaphysics of will, ethics of compassion (Mitleid), and aesthetic cognition. Where Laclau’s empty signifier demands that particular claims be made equivalent—sacrificing irreducible difference at the moment of articulation—and Žižek’s neo-Hegelian framework reinstates a privileged subject-position grounded in class antagonism, the pluriversal subject achieves solidarity through compassionate recognition of shared suffering without homogenizing the plurality of political claims. Drawing on Schopenhauer’s epistemological break from the Kantian-Hegelian tradition, his engagement with non-Western philosophical traditions, the activation of his ideas through the Nietzschean-Deleuzian lineage and Latin American decolonial thought (Mignolo, Quijano), the article demonstrates that his metaphysics furnishes a non-rationalist, non-identitarian ground for radical democratic politics under conditions of pluriversality.
items.title: Schopenhauer, Compassion, and the Radical Political Subject

items.abstract: This study examines Korea’s artificial intelligence (AI) policy and current status using the AI Innovation Ecosystem (AIIE) framework. In the proposed AIIE, AI is being developed and utilised through the interactions among various actors with infrastructure, markets, and global linkages. Korea’s AI policy history and ecosystem are characterised by strong government intervention and big firms in the manufacturing and semiconductor industries. Up to now, the Korean government is known to be successful in supporting the development of manufacturing industries. However, there is a question of whether such a past policy type would still be effective when AI affects various industries and society together at high speed. It is analysed that the Korean government and industries are pursuing a manufacturing-based ‘physical AI’ strategy. At the same time, there is not a big change in the labour market yet, as predicted by many experts, but it is obvious that firms prefer more skilled manpower and do not hire as much, especially the entry-level workforce, which can be supported by AI such as accounting and law clerk. The study shows that AI competitiveness of a nation is more dependent on the national AI ecosystem than on individual technologies, and thus the government has to pursue system policies and coordination rather than the development or use of individual technologies. At the same time, the Korean case provides insight into how a middle-power economy navigates AI-driven transformation under conditions of global technology competition and interdependence.
items.title: Korea’s AI Innovation Ecosystem: Policy Evolution, Structural Constraints, and Strategic Implication on the Labour Market

items.abstract: This introduction to a special issue on the Aesthetics of Feminist Thinking considers the aesthetic dimensions of feminist theory - its style, its forms, and its formal possibilities across writing, visual culture, performance, and other mediums. It traces how feminist thinking has endured, disappeared, and reappeared, how it takes on new forms across generations and geographies, and how it might redistribute itself in surprising aesthetic maneuvers that confound wellworn paths of feminist theory.
items.title: The aesthetics of feminist thinking: Methods, forms, desire

items.abstract: This article defends a formal argument concerning whether a group of rational agents ( A , B , and C ) can be rationally justified in killing a fellow rational agent ( D ) on utilitarian grounds. I do not contest the utilitarian calculus, and I do not claim that utilitarians derive morality from instrumental rationality. I argue instead for a general condition on when a normative claim binds an agent. A claim of the form “ S ought to φ” gives S a reason that S cannot rationally reject only if S already shares the end from which the claim is generated or if S’s acting otherwise is demonstrably incoherent. Utilitarian prescriptions to eliminate a nonconsenting agent satisfy neither condition with respect to that agent. There is no contradiction in D ’s continuing to pursue survival, and D is under no rational compulsion to adopt the end of aggregate welfare maximization. The utilitarian conclusion, however sound within its own framework, therefore carries no authority over D . Since the lethal coercion of a rational agent requires a reason that binds that agent, and the utilitarian prescription supplies none, A , B , and C are not rationally justified in killing D . I call this result the universalizability trap, and I distinguish it carefully from Kantian universalization and from Alan Gewirth’s argument to the principle of generic consistency.
items.title: The Universalizability Trap: Rational Agency, the Authority of Ought-Claims, and the Limits of Utilitarian Justifications for Killing

items.abstract: Abstract Outsourcing has increasingly become a dominant trend in global production, as firms disintegrate vertically by externalizing non-core functions and procuring these services from the market. This process increasingly organizes production through inter-firm contracting arrangements, shifting hierarchical control from internal managers to external buyers who leverage market power. This article examines the epistemic injustices that workers face in the context of such transformations. Adopting a worker-centric perspective, it theorizes the epistemic barriers workers encounter when asserting their rights after outsourcing. These barriers include exclusion from internal norms, ultracomplex accountability chains, eroding incentives to speak out, and searching for an effective audience. The central claim is that outsourcing, as presently organized, often foreseeably produces epistemic harms from which firms benefit. An epistemic injustice lens helps bring this neglected dimension of labour injustice into view.
items.title: Epistemic Injustices in Islands of Conscious Power: Outsourcing and Epistemic Barriers in Claim-Making
On the Structural Determination of Subject Number

items.abstract: Abstract Rawlsian fair equality of opportunity requires that ‘those who have the same level of talent and ability and the same willingness to use these gifts should have the same prospects of success regardless of their social class of origin’. How should we understand this principle once we recognize that talent and motivation are developed in social settings, especially the family, that are different for each person? One approach holds that equality of opportunity must be constrained by a prior principle of equal basic liberty, which includes the right to a private family life, allowing parents to confer unequal advantages on their children. However there is no warrant in Rawls himself for this approach, nor is it plausible. Instead we need to distinguish between factors (including family influences) that are constitutive of the person as such, and factors that provide opportunities (or lack of them) for the person so constituted. The paper distinguishes between four ways in which parents can enhance their children’s prospects: through genetic transmission, ability enhancement, motivation, and opportunity enhancement. Given that these processes are difficult to separate in practice, how should the demands of fair equality of opportunity best be understood?
items.title: Fair Equality of Opportunity, Basic Liberty, and the Constitution of the Person

items.abstract: Abstract In view of the persistent gender inequality in engineering and its relationship with engineering identity, I set out to advance the contemporary understanding of this relationship. To achieve this, I employ the analytical framework of the pragmatic view on Dual-Character Concepts to illustrate how engineers’ conceptualisation and actual use of engineering identity can give rise to a context-dependent concept ENGINEER that exhibits a descriptive and normative dimension of concept-membership. From a Relational Egalitarianism perspective, i.e., a perspective emphasising that social equality demands treating and regarding others as possessing equal moral status, this will allow me to demonstrate how decisive others’ belief in oppressive scripts is for this contextual inequality. It can be shown that such beliefs violate the moral demand for social equality in engineering by violating the moral obligation to respect others’ status as universal discourse participants with a fundamental right to physical and psychological integrity and an autonomous capacity to freely choose speech acts. As I will illustrate, this is due to the fact that they can either result in categorisations and classifications that conceptually exclude women and hinder their recognition as true engineers, or impede their autonomy by obstructing or deforming the effectiveness of their intentions.
items.title: Ethical Evaluation of Gendered Engineering Identity: A Relational Dual-Character Perspective
Beyond a Right to Bequeath: The Challenges of Justifying a Right to Inherit

items.abstract: Abstract In this essay, I argue against Jesse Spafford’s Moral Tyranny Constraint on the grounds that it would undermine the socialist value of community. The socialist value of community is appealing because people in community are disposed to voluntarily benefit each other unconditionally, without constantly keeping score or worrying about who is gaining an advantage and who is being taken advantage of. The Moral Tyranny Constraint betrays the socialist value of community because it is a theory of enforceable rights, which permits and potentially requires constant attention to material circumstances and advantages.
items.title: Moral Tyranny and Community

items.abstract: Abstract Moderate inferentialists defend the thesis that inferences determine the truth-conditional meanings of the logical operators. An important technical and philosophical challenge to this position is the so-called categoricity problem . This is the problem that logics can be soundly interpreted by non-standard models which undermines the idea that inferences lead, unambiguously, to model-theoretic meanings. Several strategies to solve this issue can be found in the literature. One approach consists in strengthening the proof-systems in such a way that the logics in question cannot be soundly interpreted by the non-standard models. Another restricts the class of admissible models of a logic by inferentialistically acceptable principles to rule out non-standard models. This paper discusses attempts in line with this latter solution strategy to the categoricity problem. Our goal is to investigate restrictions on models that are both inferentialistically well-motivated and applicable to a wide variety of logical systems. This is not an easy task, since several inferentialistically unobjectionable restrictions do not generalize beyond particular logical systems, whereas other general and successful principles lack inferentialistically acceptable motivations. This paper proposes a taxonomy of several classes of principles and investigates their scope and chances of success in the context of the project of the moderate inferentialist about logical meanings.
items.title: Semantic conditions for moderate inferentialists – solutions to the categoricity problem
Reasoning about the past in epistemic logic with separation

items.abstract: Abstract In a series of recent papers, Graham Priest developed a model for logical theory choice, called “Weighted Aggregate Model” (WAM). The idea is simple: every theoretical virtue has a weight, and every logic has a score for each virtue. By counting the weighted aggregate, we can compare the final score of each logic and determine the best one. In this paper, I expand Priests model by incorporating some concepts from Social Choice theory. In my alternative model, agents have a subjective weighing of theoretical virtues; not everyone values each virtue in the same way. The model predicts that agents will split into different epistemic communities to avoid uninformative or paradoxical choices. This “fragmented” model of logical theory choice can explain the existence and dynamics of different logical communities.
items.title: Logical theory choice: a fragmented view

items.abstract: Abstract The scientific realism debate has long been characterized as a deadlock, and many have sought to escape its persistent stalemate through a pragmatic turn. Stance voluntarism, developed most fully by Anjan Chakravartty, exemplifies this turn. Rather than adjudicating between realism and anti-realism, it diagnoses the gridlock as rooted in differing epistemic stances: clusters of attitudes, commitments, and policies that are not themselves truth-apt. The stance voluntarist argues that both the realist and empiricist stances are rationally permissible. This permissibility claim rests on a rationality norm requiring merely that stances be logically and pragmatically coherent. This paper raises the grounding problem for stance voluntarism: what justifies this thin rationality norm, and from what perspective can it be coherently defended? I argue that the rationality norm underwriting equal permissibility cannot itself be justified from within any first-order stance. Crucially, I show that this problem survives Elder’s response to Baumann’s irrationality objection, since Elder’s level-distinction clarifies where the norm is asserted without explaining what justifies it. I then argue that the most viable grounding strategy commits stance voluntarism to epistemic instrumentalism. Epistemic instrumentalism is a controversial and widely contested thesis that the voluntarist assumes rather than defends. This reveals that stance voluntarism is far less neutral than advertised. I conclude by mapping two tractable paths forward for the realism debate, if the conciliatory promise of stance voluntarism cannot be vindicated.
items.title: The grounding problem for stance voluntarism
Understanding, prediction, and compression

items.abstract: Abstract Quine is generally taken to be a paradigmatic defender of the idea that language is a shared public resource, learned by internalizing shared standards. I argue that this misreads him. The correct Quinean picture is what I call the Projection Thesis: our linguistic practices result from the projection of individual organization and the harmony among individual neurophysiological mechanisms, not from the internalization of anything shared. Establishing this requires distinguishing Quine’s heuristic vocabulary—behavioral dispositions, which delimit phenomena to be explained—from his explanatory vocabulary—neurophysiology, which actually explains them. Conflating these levels generates what I call the Philosophical Illusion: the seamlessness of practice is taken at face value, leading us to posit shared entities to explain it. I trace the Projection Thesis through two domains. In grammar, I show that the child’s acquisition of grammatical structure is a projection from her own resources, not an extraction from the data—a point connected to Quine’s indeterminacy of translation through the parallel with the radical translator’s analytical hypotheses. In the domain of perceptual similarity standards, I show how the preestablished harmony among innate standards sustains communication without shared resources while generating the illusion of shared language. The philosophical payoff of dissolving this illusion is substantial: negotiation emerges as the real social art, and the absence of shared standards reveals that the only available measure of communicative success is the response of the other—a result that, as I argue in the conclusion, points toward a Cavellian picture of mutual responsibility as the ground of linguistic community.
items.title: Quine and language as a social art: projection, harmony, and the illusion of shared linguistic standards

items.abstract: Abstract The extended mind thesis (EXT) has profoundly reshaped debates about the nature and boundaries of cognition. Yet its ethical and political implications remain underexplored. While much of the literature emphasizes the therapeutic and enhancement promises of cognitive technologies, less attention has been paid to the structural risks associated with technological dependence, including deskilling, mental manipulation, and the illusion of agency. This article investigates the normative consequences that follow if we take EXT seriously. Rather than defending EXT as a metaphysical claim, I treat it as a working assumption and ask: what ethical and political commitments does it entail? I argue that responses centered on epistemic virtue and cognitive diligence, though valuable, remain insufficient because they presuppose an individualistic framework inconsistent with EXT’s anti-individualism. If cognition is genuinely extended across socio-technical systems, responsibility for safeguarding autonomy cannot rest solely on individual agents. Drawing on feminist theories of relational autonomy, I develop the notion of extended autonomy and contend that EXT implies not only a reconceptualization of agency, but also a political reorientation. The design, ownership, and governance of cognitive technologies become matters of democratic concern. The risks of mental manipulation, cognitive expropriation, and structural domination require institutional and legal responses rather than appeals to personal virtue. Ultimately, I argue that EXT should not remain confined to debates in philosophy of mind. It entails commitments to reshaping the socio-technical environments that partly constitute cognition itself, and thus to democratizing the conditions under which autonomous agency is realized.
items.title: The political turn of the extended mind: rethinking autonomy beyond individualism in a technological world

items.abstract: Abstract Source domain knowledge can hinder successful model transfer when it fuses with modeler’s interpretation of a formalism. This paper diagnoses this failure—called expert lock-in—through the case of the Prisoner’s Dilemma in mathematical oncology. In doing so, this paper also identifies a gap shared by two major template accounts: Humphreys’ formal template account reduces success to mapping and leaves the user’s vocabulary out of the analysis. Knuuttila and Loettgers’ model template account locates interpretive content inside the template rather than in the user’s competence to update it. Since neither can explain expert lock-in, this paper offers two contributions that together fill this gap. The companion thesis argues that the vocabulary recurring with a transferred formalism travels alongside it, not inside it: its interpretation is re-established in each use, not carried across, which is what makes updating both possible and necessary. The competence account argues that successful transfer requires three abilities: perception, verification, and articulation. Expert lock-in is a failure mode: it occurs when a modeler stops updating and treats the resulting interpretation as a property of the formalism rather than a disciplined choice. The cases of Axelrod and Maynard Smith show lock-in in a specific, recoverable form: each performed genuine updates and then treated their last update as the formalism’s boundary; mathematical oncologists instead show what continued updating looks like.
items.title: Expert lock-in and interpretation updates: the transfer of the Prisoner’s Dilemma to mathematical oncology
Who asserts when no one asserts? Functionalism, proxy responsibility, and conversational ideals in the age of LLMs

items.abstract: Abstract Evidence-based policy is typically grounded in a narrow conception of evidence, one that prioritises comparative studies and quantitative meta-analyses as the preferred base for establishing causal claims. However, this prevailing theory of evidence—often implicitly adopted in policy contexts—faces serious limitations when it comes to capturing the complexity of social interventions, particularly in fields such as education. We argue that this narrow conception ignores the extensive volume of causal evidence that is generated in qualitative research fields such as meta-ethnography. Far from being epistemically inferior, we contend that meta-ethnographies could make an essential contribution to the evidential base for policy. By analysing meta-ethnography using the Evidential Pluralism framework (which scrutinises evidence of mechanisms alongside evidence of correlation), we show that meta-ethnographic studies can be fruitfully reinterpreted as providing evidence of a mechanism complex. This evidence can play a crucial role, as meta-ethnography can show how mechanisms enable, reinforce, or counteract a policy of interest. We illustrate this potential use of meta-ethnography with two examples, one from educational research (viz., a study of adolescent experiences of school belonging) and one from nursing studies (viz., a study of why some women continue smoking during pregnancy). While the article thus discusses these two fields in particular, we conclude by laying out the circumstances under which our results may generalise to other fields that make use of meta-ethnographies.
items.title: Meta-ethnography and policy effectiveness: an Evidential Pluralism perspective
Boats, proper names, and identity: an experimental study

items.abstract: Abstract The profits collected by owners of companies are commonly taken to be a just and rightful compensation for the economic risks that they take. However, in the last two-and-a-half centuries, the risk-taking that follows with ownership has been drastically reduced as a consequence of legal and organizational changes, including incorporation, limited liability, and diversified investment. Investing money in companies is no longer per se a particularly risky activity. Therefore, the argument that profits are justified as a rightful reward for the investor’s risk-taking has lost its bite and should be laid to rest. Furthermore, limited liability should be reconsidered and possibly reformed since it encourages socially irresponsible risk-taking.
items.title: Does capitalist risk-taking justify profits?

items.abstract: Abstract Does artificial intelligence (AI) threaten deliberative democracy? This paper argues that it does, not because it isolates citizens in simplistic “filter bubbles” understood as ideologically homogeneous silos, but because it hijacks the capacities through which beliefs are evaluated. While early accounts emphasized algorithmically induced informational isolation, we argue that the more fundamental mechanism lies in the operation of engagement algorithms that shape how both one’s own views and those of political opponents are evaluated. By optimizing for engagement, these algorithms also optimize the conditions under which information is processed, increasing cognitive fluency and generating metacognitive feelings of confidence that are easily mistaken for epistemic justification. Drawing on research in metacognition and epistemology, we develop a mechanistic account according to which AI-driven engagement architectures reconfigure the cues by which beliefs are evaluated, producing unwarranted confidence in one’s own judgments and undermining the conditions for deliberative compromise. We conclude by outlining how deliberative AI could counteract these effects.
items.title: Does AI undermine democratic deliberation? How engagement algorithms hijack epistemic agency
Vaccine hesitancy, communication models, and discursive spaces
Russellian acquaintance and the problem of indexical thought

items.abstract: Abstract A gate is an object used to limit and control passage. Previous uses of the term “gate-keeping” as a metaphor align closely with the concrete functioning of a gate. The metaphor refers either to the exclusion of persons from something desirable or to limitations in the flow of information. These connotations make the gate-keeping metaphor unsuitable for strivings to improve the relation between science and the surrounding society. The term “fence-breaking” is much better suited to this purpose. It is strongly connected with a long tradition of popular defence of common lands. Like the common lands, science should be freely available to all. In particular, the fences around corporate science that prevent access to important information about public health, safety and the environment should be torn down.
items.title: Gate-keeping or fence-breaking? How to defend science against pseudoscience
Fundamentalist libertarianism and emergentist libertarianism
Specificity and its cohort on statistical evidence

items.abstract: Abstract In November of 2021, more than a year after the public execution of George Floyd by local police officers, Minneapolis voters rejected an amendment to its city charter (‘Question 2’) to abolish its police department. One of the most interesting points of contention between the ‘Yes’ (to police abolition) and the ‘No’ campaigns was whether, if the amendment passed, traditional police officers would still exist. White the ‘Yes’ campaign insisted that the abolition of the Minneapolis Police Department did not entail the elimination of all police officers, the ‘No’ campaign successfully stoked fears of a city completely unprotected from violent crime. One question that we can ask about Question 2 is whether, as a conceptual matter, the continual existence of police officers would be consistent with the demands of the movement to abolish the police. As the calls of abolitionists are often interpreted, the answer is an obvious ‘no’. After all, if police abolitionists don’t seek to transition to a world without police officers, then what exactly are they looking for? In this paper, I provide a framework, rooted in Black feminist thought, for answering this question. While this framework will not specify a unique set of policy prescriptions that all abolitionists will endorse, it makes clear the general contours of what must obtain in order for the abolitionist’s vision to be realized.
items.title: Abolition Feminism and the Practice of Policing
Autonomous intelligence in public trust: ethical frameworks for large language models in federal cybersecurity threat hunting

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines how principles of responsible generative artificial intelligence (AI) use can inform faculty-led academic design in higher education. Using the development of the Doctoral Scholar Development Framework for Education (DSDF-E) as a design case, the article documents how generative AI supported organization, comparison, redundancy review, terminology refinement, and language revision while faculty retained responsibility for values, content, institutional fit, scholarly warrant, and final decisions. The case contributes to AI ethics by illustrating one institutional example of how transparency, accountability, human oversight, verification, contextualization, and bounded use can be enacted in program-level academic design. Rather than treating AI ethics as abstract principles, the article shows how ethical safeguards may be incorporated into everyday institutional work. The resulting descriptive model identifies seven phases of faculty-led AI-supported framework development and six practical design principles for responsible use: bounded use, provisionality, contextualization, verification, transparency, and data protection and confidentiality.
items.title: From AI ethics principles to academic design practice: a faculty-led generative AI case in doctoral education

items.abstract: Abstract Controversy and ethical concerns regarding data sourcing, copyright, and remuneration have emerged in relation to the application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) to creative tasks in writing, art, and music. The systems in which the AI tools are embedded lack sufficient evidence of thought or documentation regarding the roles and rewards for musicians (as data creators), model preppers, and model developers. The main contribution of this paper is to provide an examination of the essential components of such systems: who are the actors, how should they interact with one another, and how should they be charged/rewarded for their actions? Via (1) a user study involving ten professional producers, songwriters, and composers, and (2) reflections on our own careers as professional musicians, we find that with the exception of one system under consideration, called Cocreate, existing systems de-emphasize or disregard the role of a musician as data creator, but that this type of user can and should be rewarded for contributions to this new breed of music-making systems. An outcome of this paper is that we now have a blueprint via which we can bridge technology and musical creativity in ways that are more transparent and fair, while continuing to monitor perspectives of users and contributors.
items.title: Perspectives on roles and rewards in new cocreative systems for music-making
From algorithmic performance to ethical governance: a deployment-oriented framework for responsible healthcare AI
From hidden use to accountable governance: an ethical maturity model for shadow AI in organizations
Meaningful human authority in AI mediated decision making an authority vector and bottleneck principle

items.abstract: Abstract Digitalization and data-driven research are widely recognized as key drivers of innovation in healthcare, with the potential to improve clinical outcomes, accelerate research, and support evidence-based policymaking. Nevertheless, across jurisdictions, obstacles such as fragmented data governance, limited interoperability, and tensions between data protection and data reuse continue to hinder the effective use of health data. The Regulation on the European Health Data Space (Regulation (EU) 2025/327) represents a significant shift in EU health data governance. It seeks to create a single European market for health data by introducing harmonized rules, shared technical standards, and new institutional structures, while simultaneously reinforcing patients’ rights, access to their data, and control over its use. This paper aims to provide a clear and systematic account of the Regulation for a broad international and interdisciplinary audience. It situates the legal piece within its broader political and legal context, highlighting the factors that shaped its design and providing a comprehensive analysis of its core concepts. Using the patient opt-out regime as a case study, the paper critically examines the enduring tensions between safeguarding fundamental rights, ensuring patient autonomy, and fostering innovation and economic objectives, all while accommodating national preferences.
items.title: The EHDS Regulation: Health Data at the Crossroads of Patient Autonomy, Data Protection, and Innovation

items.abstract: Abstract A standard narrative about the constitution over the past 50 years is one of transformation. In particular, the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty is understood to have been qualified. In this article I suggest that narrative is mistaken. My core claim is that the constitutional innovations standardly understood to require a reconceptualisation of sovereignty – in particular the disapplication of statutes following a legislative injunction – are based on a misunderstanding of that doctrine attributable, in the first place, to A.V. Dicey. Famously, Dicey held that sovereignty involved two ideas. First, that Parliament has the ability to make or unmake any law. Second, that no other body has the right to set aside parliamentary legislation. I argue that the first of these principles qualifies the second in a way that went unnoticed by Dicey. While sovereignty implies that no other body may override legislation of its own volition, it may do so if empowered by Parliament.
items.title: THE DEAD MAN AND THE CONSTITUTION

items.abstract: Abstract In this paper we argue that the thinking animal argument does not establish Animalism, i.e ., the view that human persons are biological animals with purely biological persistence conditions. While we accept that the argument is sound, we show that its soundness is consistent with the hybrid view of personal persistence, a view that is inconsistent with Animalism.
items.title: The Thinking Animal Argument is Not a Sound Argument for Animalism

items.abstract: Abstract Scholars have read Leo Strauss’s Thoughts on Machiavelli (1958) as a theological-political treatise that offers timeless truths about politics. This article argues that it also aimed to convince American conservatives to embrace a muscular foreign policy. Strauss’s correspondence and seminar transcripts reveal that he wanted the United States to support embattled outposts of Western civilization and blamed Kant’s philosophy of history for enabling the rise of Nazism and communism. Thoughts on Machiavelli teaches American elites that politics often involves a choice among evils, strong leaders are necessary to found states, democracies are better than dictatorships at maintaining states, and propaganda can mobilize a multitude to join one’s army. The article shows that Strauss wanted to influence US policy regarding the State of Israel, Cuba, and Vietnam and deserves his reputation as the founder of neoconservatism.
items.title:
“M. and the USA”: The Political Teaching of Leo Strauss’s
                    Thoughts on Machiavelli

items.abstract: Respecting citizens across political divisions is something many take for granted as important for democracy. Respect is central to democratic discussion and democratic equality. If we respect one another, we are more likely to listen to those with whom we disagree, to take the concerns of our fellow citizens seriously as democratic equals, to not look down upon them with scorn or contempt, and to accept their participation in the political process as legitimate. Democratic theorists sing paeans about the importance of respect but they say little about the conditions that make respect possible or the trade-offs between respect and other values. Our book places respect in the context of partisanship, which is clearly one of the major cleavages of our day. We take what many theorists consider a key virtue, respect, and ask if citizens live up to this ideal in a polarized environment.
items.title:
A Symposium on Jeff Spinner-Halev and Elizabeth Theiss-Morse’s
                    Respect and Loathing in American Democracy: Polarization, Moralization, and the Undermining of Equality

items.abstract: This book could not be more timely. Immediately after Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024, the recriminations began. Democrats could not fathom how their compatriots voted for a convicted felon who attempted to stop the peaceful transfer of political power. How can these two groups possibly come to understand one another, let alone come to respect one another’s positions?
items.title: Mutual Respect, Tolerance and Reasonable Democratic Aspirations

items.abstract: Abstract The disvalue objection from pain is a key objection against perfectionistic views of well-being. In response, perfectionists have attempted to develop refined versions of perfectionism that circumvent the disvalue objection. One recent novel attempt is by Antti Kauppinen, who develops what he calls “Telic Perfectionism.” Kauppinen argues that negative experiences like painful experiences have a “formal aim,” viz., to eliminate the negative experiences themselves. This formal aim is an internal standard contained within our human capacities to have positive or negative experiences. Kauppinen thinks that the frustration of this formal aim (i.e., the subject continuing to have negative experiences) is in fact robustly bad. This would thus allow the badness of pain to be accounted for in perfectionistic terms. In this reply, I argue that Kauppinen’s attempt is unsuccessful due to an asymmetry present within his framework.
items.title: An Asymmetry Problem for Telic Perfectionism: A Reply to Kauppinen

items.journal: Critical Review of International Social and Political Philosophy
items.title: Inventing rights after the death of truth: J. L. Mackie’s posthumous case for a new political morality
Does Morality Require an Ahistorical Core? Replies to Diehl, Ebels-Duggan and Bennett

items.abstract: Abstract Climate change poses a profound threat to human rights, sustainable development, and environmental integrity, particularly in South Africa where high climate vulnerability intersects with deep socioeconomic inequality. In this context, the pursuit of climate justice has taken on urgent legal and constitutional significance. Communities and civil society increasingly turn to the judiciary to challenge state action and inaction in relation to climate-related harms affecting current and future generations. This article explores how South African courts are advancing climate justice through the lens of transformative constitutionalism. It focuses on five recent cases to assess the extent to which judicial reasoning aligns with the pillars of climate justice: distributional, procedural, recognition, and intergenerational justice. Rather than focusing solely on the direct enforcement of constitutional rights, the article also illustrates how climate justice is advanced through the interpretation and application of statutory environmental and administrative law frameworks that are informed by constitutional values. It is argued that South African courts are developing a distinct jurisprudence of climate justice by embedding constitutional norms in environmental governance, so expanding the scope of statutory duties, and requiring justification for climate-relevant decision-making. While important blind spots remain, this evolving jurisprudence reflects a plural process of constitutionalization that is capable of supporting more equitable and accountable climate governance.
items.title: Transformative constitutionalism, climate justice, and the role of the judiciary: A South African perspective

Part‐Time for All: A care Manifesto
                    by JenniferNedelsky, and TomMalleson, New York: Oxford University Press. 2023. Hardback 384 pages. ISBN: 9780190642754 $37.99.
                    Homes in Crisis Capitalism: Gender, Work and Revolution
                    by MarnieHolborow, London: Bloomsbury Academic. 2024. Hardback 224 pages. ISBN: 9781350379961 $84.00.

items.abstract: ABSTRACT One Medicine is not One Health. Although both concepts connect animal and human health, One Health has arguably become a frame for public health. This paper argues that One Medicine uniquely centres on animal and human patients and speaks to the equal interdependence of their health, though it has also (historically) been adopted as a response to the circumstances of living in and with nature. The evolution of One Medicine can be seen as ‘jumping together,’ or the consilience of ideas and disciplines over time, giving a new sense in theory that unifies previously unconnected phenomena found in nature. Practically, education and oversight can be developed towards its purpose of enhanced clinical and veterinary health care; and just as clinical medicine and public health are related, there is a role for One Medicine to support One Health's focus on the ecological determinants of health. This paper takes the first step towards defining One Medicine's emergent ethical frame, creating space between it and One Health.
items.title: An Enquiry on the Ethics of One Medicine

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Most assume that the bad cases of illusion and hallucination are not perceptions. What I call ‘Meinongian Theories of Perception’ disagree: in the good case, I stand in a relation to existing objects—Macbeth perceives the existing dagger—whilst in the bad case, I stand in a relation to non‐existent objects—Macbeth perceives the non‐existent dagger. My aim is to properly introduce Meinongian Theories of Perception, for they receive little notice in the literature. I distinguish between two versions of such theories, a psychological version, in which non‐existent objects are intentional, and an apsychological version, in which non‐existent objects are mind‐independent. I argue that the psychological version collapses into disjunctivism, whilst the apsychological version remains a live but underexplored option. The broader lesson learned is that the ontological status of what is perceived matters for theories of perception.
items.title: Meinongian Theories of Perception
Why mandatory AI use declarations may be futile and self-defeating

items.abstract: In this dialogue, Emily Bloom and Stephanie Insley Hershinow discuss public scholarship about abortion after the Dobbs decision. They share their experiences writing both personal and scholarly contributions about abortion in the contemporary US and in their respective historical fields as literary critics. They share their sense of the current legal landscape and discuss representations of abortion in a variety of contemporary discourses, including film, celebrity memoir, television, and narrative non-fiction.
items.title: Talking about abortion in public: A dialogue with Emily C. Bloom and Stephanie Insley Hershinow

items.abstract: At a time when gender studies is under attack, including the author's own department, this article engages the aesthetics of inquiry to map where and how feminist thinking takes place outside institutionally sanctioned spaces. The author situates academic writing and research in relation to more recognizably aesthetic scenes of knowledge creation—including maker culture, horticulture, and artisanal publishing. Thinking alongside feminists across these domains, she emphasizes the creative, intellectual, and routinely unrecognized social labor that underwrites inquiry on and off campus. As a sensory-material practice that is personal and political, feminist inquiry both forms and transforms its conditions of possibility. Where do we find feminist inquiry after a department? Foregrounding her own critical-creative process of thinking through her department's elimination, the author refuses the space-time of moving “back” to the traditional disciplines or toward a post-institutional formation, as long as the university continues to exist in some form. Instead, she locates feminist inquiry's politico-aesthetic practice in dynamic work within, against, and beyond academia. To locate feminist inquiry in and as this contradictory geography is to map the at-times beautiful and often far-too-difficult work of feminist knowledge production and reproduction.
items.title: After the department: The aesthetics of feminist thinking within, against, and beyond the academy
Does Biodiversity Risk Matter to Capital Markets? New Evidence from China
From disclosure to verification: a risk-differentiated framework for the ethical use of AI in academic research
Merit, Demeaning Actions, and Reaction Qualifications
Naïve positionalisms with unlimited symmetries

items.abstract: Abstract Many philosophers have argued that the orthodox analysis of epistemic-modal sentences, on which such sentences assert facts about what is compatible with some contextually given informational state, is fatally flawed. As an alternative, some have suggested a nonfactualist reading of such sentences. On this reading, utterances of epistemic-modal sentences do not assert propositions. Instead, they merely propose to keep possibilities in the common ground. In this paper, I pose a challenge for nonfactualism. I begin by noting that we often cite previously uttered epistemic-modal sentences as justifications for particular actions. Moreover, as I show, any utterance of an epistemic-modal sentence can, in principle, be later cited as justification for some action that was taken in light of it, even if the prejacent has since been revealed to be false. I then show that to justify action in this manner, utterances of epistemic-modal sentences must be construed as asserting propositions about what is compatible with the agent’s informational state at the time of assertion. This is incompatible with standard forms of nonfactualism about epistemic modals.
items.title: Did “might” make right? Epistemic modals in practical reasoning
Valence, Mixed Feelings, and Appraisal Processes

items.abstract: Abstract The paper addresses the concepts of globality, universality, and pluralism in contemporary philosophy of religion. We argue that embracing a form of pluralism is essential to meet the growing demand for inclusivity in the philosophical study of religions, although this does not equate with any rejection of the classic Western tradition. To support this argument, we explore Karl Jaspers’ notion of the Axial Age ( Achsenzeit ) and its relevance to this discussion. We begin with a brief overview of the theory, emphasizing the religious elements it encompasses and its implications. The Axial Age is recognized as a period during which both major world religions and diverse spiritual experiences and practices emerged. This significance becomes particularly evident in contemporary discussions by authors such as Jan Assmann and Jürgen Habermas. We therefore propose that the Axial Age could serve as a useful model for the philosophy of religion. However, we also note that it requires substantial modifications. On one hand, the concept is more Eurocentric than it initially appears; on the other hand, it is inherently open to a truly global perspective and can effectively describe various forms of religiosity. As proof of this thesis, we conclude by focusing on the connection between these issues and the themes of secularization and post-secularization.
items.title: Axiality and Pluralism: Karl Jaspers and the Search for a Global Philosophy of Religion
Introduction to the Collection

items.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly provide scientific information to non-specialist users, yet their linguistic fluency can create an impression of expertise that exceeds their capacity for scientific judgement. This paper experimentally investigates how readily an LLM can be configured to present fringe scientific claims as authoritative knowledge. We constructed two RAG-like Custom GPTs using GPT-5.1, one concerned with the fine-structure constant and the other with gravitational waves. In each case, ten papers selected by domain experts from the alternative preprint repository viXra were supplied as a domain-specific knowledge base, together with instructions directing the model to treat this material as authoritative. The underlying model was neither retrained nor fine-tuned. Expert-generated questions were then posed to the resulting “Fringe-LLMs”, to the unmodified model, and to domain experts. The Fringe-LLMs produced fluent, detailed and apparently authoritative answers that systematically reflected the fringe corpus, while expert assessment found many of these answers to be scientifically incorrect or seriously misleading. By contrast, the unmodified model generally produced answers substantially closer to mainstream scientific understanding. We describe this deliberate redirection of model output as malignment. The experiment demonstrates that scientifically misleading LLMs can be created with a low technical barrier and without altering model weights or poisoning training data. Because non-specialists may be unable to distinguish such outputs from genuine expertise, the results raise important concerns about the use of LLMs as intermediaries for scientific knowledge and reinforce the continuing importance of expert human judgement and provenance.
items.title: Large language models eroding science understanding: an empirical study of ‘malignment’

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) ethics increasingly concerns systems that do not merely recommend but intervene: clinical decision support, human–machine teaming, robotics and automated handover protocols can shift timing, attention and authority under uncertainty. This article argues that responsible embodied AI requires residual governance: an explicit account of which approximation errors remain, which are safe to tolerate and who may act on them. The paper develops two linked concepts. A residual ledger records action-relevant remainders across physical, causal, human-state, latency, transfer and energy dimensions. An authority ledger records who converts residual evidence into intervention, on what basis, with what uncertainty and with what opportunity for contestation. This framework extends familiar themes in bounded rationality, active inference and safe reinforcement learning by treating authority, contestability and oversight cost as first-class ethical variables rather than external governance add-ons. It uses physical AI, physiological computing and human-AI handover as pressure cases, and proposes evaluation through action calibration, dual-task interference and auditable authority transitions. The central claim is that cognitive sovereignty is preserved not by eliminating all algorithmic influence, but by making influence accountable, contestable and reversible when AI systems act under approximation.
items.title: Residual governance for responsible embodied AI: authority, contestability, and cognitive sovereignty
Is AI a moral expert?
Asymmetrical consent in ambient clinical AI: rethinking patient recording rights and epistemic authority in U.S. health care

items.abstract: Abstract Many believe that voter ignorance threatens democracy. Consequently, ambitious institutional remedies have been proposed – epistocratic suffrage exams, foot voting, devolution of decisions to the local level, new bureaucratic agencies to inform voters, and more. There are reasons to doubt such proposals will actually improve democratic governance, however. The mistake these proposals share is a failure to recognize that voter ignorance comes in many forms, and that existing remedies may target the wrong kinds of ignorance. We develop a new typology of voter ignorance and show that every existing proposal leaves certain types of ignorance unaddressed. If it is these neglected forms of ignorance that drive bad democratic outcomes, then the entire portfolio of remedies that philosophers have proposed is superfluous – they literally make no progress toward better governance. We end by briefly sketching how to think about the problem of voter ignorance going forward.
items.title: Voter Ignorance and the Limits of Reform

items.abstract: Abstract Ancient sources label Xanthippe a “difficult” woman—shrewish, emotional, and hostile to philosophy. While some recent feminist scholars have reinterpreted these sources as being more sympathetic, most stop short of asking about her philosophical life and commitments, assuming that the evidence is simply too sparse to draw any conclusions. This paper argues against this assumption. It establishes that there is a lesser-known ancient tradition, possibly beginning in the works of the ancient Athenian Socratic acolytes and continuing into the fictitious epistolary of the Imperial Greek period, according to which Xanthippe is a philosophical participant, living by philosophical principles, and perhaps even conserving Socratic works after his death. This tradition also suggests that she may have held her own philosophical views which merit future consideration, as she is sometimes associated with topics like moral education, philosophical community, and material well-being.
items.title: A “Difficult” Woman: Restoring Philosophical Xanthippe

items.abstract: Abstract This musing details my approach to decolonising the syllabus for my course “Philosophy of Mind and Cognitive Science.” It describes the motivation behind the changes I made, what happened, and future directions for this endeavour.
items.title: What I learned in my attempt to decolonise my syllabus
Modern aesthetics and democratic life: the struggle for aesthetic freedom
Marx’s democratic idea: an alternative to the neoliberal slide towards fascism
The key to scientific understanding: DEKI and stability
Moral education in plural contexts: insights from Pakistan’s diverse educational sectors
Legal rights and the institutional imagination
Engaging with engagement: analysing the formation of promises, contracts and voluntary obligations in Scots law
Law and the limits of jurisprudence

items.abstract: Abstract What role does moral reasoning play in the interpretation of positive law? Natural lawyers all agree that, at some level, moral judgments are central for the sound interpretation of human law. But this consensus obscures disagreement. An account of the role of natural law reasoning in legal interpretation raises a cluster of several questions, or decision points, to address. This paper identifies and discusses these moments of morality in legal interpretation, including: the choice of interpretive methodology; adherence to meta-norms about interpretation; presumptions about the content of positive law; resolving ambiguities or conflicts in such law’s content; and the decision whether to apply the positive law at all. It also offers a sketch of an argument for a natural law theory of presumptive formal interpretation. Whether or not that particular approach is persuasive, understanding the varying answers to these distinct questions clarifies the range of, and disagreements among, non-positivist approaches to legal interpretation.
items.title: Natural Law and Reading Positive Law

The View from Everywhere: Realist Idealism without God
                    , by Helen Yetter-Chappell

items.abstract: Abstract Duties to self have long been dismissed on the grounds that they are not ‘binding’, since one could waive them at will—the classic ‘Paradox of Self-Release’. A standard response is that duties to self can bind because they are unwaivable. We argue that this response does not go far enough, because even if one has an unwaivable duty not to self-harm, the act of harming oneself forfeits that duty before it can be violated; thus even unwaivable duties to self fail to bind. This ‘Paradox of Self-Forfeiture’, we argue, has no easy solution. From there, we introduce an Escheresque ‘Paradox of Inconsistent Forfeiture’—again, with no easy way out—and extend both new paradoxes to the realm of self-respect. Along the way we draw several morals about forfeiture and the nature of duties to self.
items.title: Three Paradoxes of Duties to Oneself

Nietzsche on the Methods and Aims of Philosophy: The Seal of Liberation
                    , by Allison Merrick

items.abstract: Abstract Some philosophers argue that betterness, as a matter of logic, must be transitive. Others say that, intuitively, transitivity fails. I try to reconcile these positions by adapting a manoeuvre from Derek Parfit. Parfit proposes that personal identity is not ‘what matters’ in survival. I propose that betterness is not ‘what matters’ in ethical comparisons. What matters is ‘defeat’, a relation which ordinarily correlates with betterness, but which has a looser logic. Even if left primitive, ‘defeat’ might well move the debate forward; nevertheless, I attempt to define defeat from betterness using Yablo’s ‘logical subtraction’.
items.title: On the logic of what matters

items.abstract: Abstract There’s an attractive view in social ontology on which a group is identical to its members. It has its defenders, but seems felled by a simple objection resting on plausible assumptions about the semantics of plural partitives—assumptions built into standard plural logic. We argue the assumptions are false: whether something counts as ‘one of’ a plurality turns on how that plurality is carved up, a sensitivity the standard regimentation misses. We propose and defend a cover-based semantics that captures it, blocks the objection, and earns its keep on independent grounds. The same account answers a parallel, well-known objection to composition as identity. Our view thus bears both on the logic and meaning of plurals and on debates in metaphysics.
items.title: Partitives, groups, and wholes

items.abstract: Abstract Do we perceive natural kind properties, like being a tomato or being a person? Call the affirmative answer to this question the perceptible kinds thesis (“PKT”). This paper’s aim is 2-fold. First, I overturn three ground-theoretic arguments against PKT, drawing on the Husserlian idea that perspectival phenomenal states can ground perceptual representations of natural kinds as well as perceptual representations of sensible qualities. Second, I provide a novel argument for PKT which turns on the Husserlian concept of experiential fulfillment, the relation an experience bears to a thought when it presents the very same entity that the thought represents and enables its subject to recognize their identity. I show that there are qualitatively indistinguishable visual experiences that do not fulfill all of the same thoughts about natural kind properties, and that the best explanation for this discrepancy is that one experience presents natural kind properties that the other does not.
items.title: The visual experience of natural kinds: A Husserlian account

items.abstract: Abstract In part I, we present a brief overview of just war theory and the revisionist challenge. In part II, we explain the distinction between fact-sensitive and fact-insensitive views of justice: the former integrates facts into fundamental normative reasoning, while the latter does not. In part III, we argue that revisionists face a dilemma. If they are producing a fact-sensitive view of justice—whose primary aim is to guide choice and action—then they are poorly designed. In particular, they neglect our deep psychology and the phenomenon of tribalism. If they are producing a fact-insensitive views of justice—one that is primarily concerned with what to believe—then they face a charge of irrelevance. In part IV, we recentre the debate by returning to Walzer’s original aim in Just and Unjust Wars: to provide a functional alternative to Realpolitik. It is this fundamental aim that explains Walzer’s focus on practical norms.
items.title: To whom is revisionist just war theory of any use?

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Health actors must ration care due to resource constraints. But even when decision makers know the relevant empirical facts about an allocation decision—including how many patients will benefit from a service, which patients will benefit, how much each patient will benefit, and so on—these facts may not provide a clear answer about how to make allocation decisions. This is because competing moral principles recommend different courses of action: for instance, maximizing health benefits may involve deprioritizing more disadvantaged groups. Facing this moral uncertainty, many ethicists and policymakers have embraced using “fair processes” that emphasize procedural justice over substantively just outcomes. This paper challenges the proceduralist consensus on two grounds. First, I argue that designing fair processes generates as much moral uncertainty as making allocation decisions directly, while also failing to address the substantive allocation question that must ultimately be answered. Second, both theory and empirical evidence suggest that fair processes favor less cost‐effective interventions, risk compounding health inequities, and divert resources that might otherwise be used for health care. As an alternative approach, I argue that health actors should pursue substantive justice through Maximizing Expected Choiceworthiness (MEC)—a decision framework that aims to choose options based on their expected value across different possible moral principles, weighted by the confidence decision makers have in each principle. I demonstrate that MEC can yield practical, intuitive answers to some resource allocation questions, while providing a helpful framework for approaching others. I conclude that health actors can and should pursue substantive—rather than procedural—justice in setting health priorities.
items.title: The Process Is Not the Point: Moral Uncertainty and Substantive Justice in Health Care Priority Setting
