items.abstract: ABSTRACT I argue that a Zhuangzian approach offers philosophical resources to address normative issues related to physical and sensory disability. In so doing, I roughly endorse Yong Huang's interpretation of the Zhuangzi . This ethical groundwork allows for an exploration of how we can understand disability. I also argue that the Zhuangzi 's notions of the equality of things, the challenge of binaries (e.g. useful/useless), transformation and change, and the moral principle imply an ethics of disability that merits consideration vis‐à‐vis other normative theories of disability. This is because this theory can address certain limitations of the medical and social models of disability. Examples include failing to recognise the impact of social conventions or exaggerating such conventions and emphasising the relevance of physical impairment.
items.title: Pragmatism and Authenticity beyond the Social and Medical Models: A Zhuangzian Approach to Physical and Sensory Disability

items.abstract: Abstract In a recent article, Jonathan Seglow and Matteo Bonotti develop an interesting and original relational approach to free speech—one that grounds the value of (protecting) large swathes of speech in the relational need that we have for ‘recognition’ from those around us, and the role speech plays in facilitating recognition. Here, I argue that while their argument provides an exciting foundation for a relational free speech account, it may not be able to provide a stern rebuke to certain cases of censorship that we would want a free speech account to rebuke. I have in mind here cases where censorship will have little to no impact on an agent’s ability to give and receive meaningful recognition. In addition, like all relational accounts, their account relies on the idea that human beings are social animals with relational needs. But what their account does not provide, and what is indeed something of a lacuna in relational accounts more generally, is a sense of whether our social nature is a gift or a curse. Fortunately, we can respond to both problems by considering how speech facilitates other kinds of relational goods, beyond securing our need for recognition. By way of example, I discuss the integral role speech plays in enabling us to meet our moral duties to help those around us, and how this provides a relational argument for protecting certain kinds of speech that may not be protected by a narrower, recognition-based relational approach. But this is just one example in service of a more general lesson. It is sometimes said that the best kind of free speech argument would be of a ‘patchwork’ form—stitching together different free speech arguments in favour of protecting different kinds of speech (say a truth-based argument in favour of protecting academic speech, an intellectual autonomy-based argument for protecting artistic speech, and so on). It may be that we can stitch together a patchwork of purely relational arguments in order to provide an extensive, cohesive account of the value of speech. This is an exciting prospect for relational theorists. Still, to do this, we will need to attend to the full range of our relational needs and how they intertwine with speech.
items.title: Relational Free Speech Reconsidered

items.abstract: Abstract Several philosophers have recently debated whether something called ‘epistemic blame’ exists. Others have proposed that there also exists ‘aesthetic blame’, ‘epistemic praise’, ‘epistemic atonement’, ‘epistemic hypocrisy’, and it isn’t hard to imagine others still arguing for the existence of things like ‘zetetic blame’ or ‘athletic blame’. This paper proposes that arguments from both realists and sceptics about such phenomena misunderstand the nature of blame and other components of our accountability practices. Although epistemic blame (etc.) sceptics are correct that epistemic blame does not exist, epistemic blame realists are correct that ‘moral blame’ is insufficient for helping make sense of our reactions to agents who violate epistemic norms. Once we understand that blame’s function is norm-enforcement simpliciter, we have no need to posit distinct forms of blame (praise, forgiveness, etc.). Despite seeming revisionary, the position maintains all the argumentative strengths of both realism and scepticism, with few drawbacks. It also renders our understanding of blame consistent with independently convincing accounts of epistemic normativity, and both epistemic and moral norms.
items.title: There is no such thing as epistemic, aesthetic, athletic, zetetic, or even moral blame

items.abstract: Abstract When considering new forms of technological innovation, they are often given varying labels such as “emerging”, “disruptive”, or “critical”. However, nowhere is the literature more divided on the parameters of technological inclusion than in the field of “dual-use” technologies. Conceptually, dual-use technologies have a dichotomous characteristic: they can used for civilian purpose as well as in defence or military applications. But where do the boundaries lie? For example, are law enforcement, surveillance or espionage uses of new technologies deemed “civilian” or “military” in nature? Further, the labelling of a technology as “dual-use” is incredibly significant – it can trigger classification of research data or the imposition of export controls, making collaborative efforts and publications on that technology more difficult as researchers navigate a torturous process of governmental encroachment, licensing, and regulation. This paper proposes a radical shift in innovation policy: discarding dual-use as a label of technology. Instead, it proposes a more nuanced framework which encourages more granular discussions about the potential national and economic security implications of a given technological development. The paper goes on to argue for the analytical and empirical value of that framework through application in contextual case studies derived from classification and export control cases globally. This paper therefore frames dual-use as an unhelpful metaphor in technology policy and encourages the literature and industry of research move to a more helpful framework for discussing new technologies.
items.title: Describing a Novel Framework to Replace Dual-Use as a Technological Label
The Battlefield of Indeterminate Causation and its Additivity
Pseudo-consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: a functional and governance framework for consciousness-like systems

items.abstract: Abstract There has recently been a movement in AI research to go beyond ‘human-centered AI’, and to consider whether and how AI systems should promote non-anthropocentric values or values that go beyond human concerns. However, the research domain of automated machine learning (AutoML) lags behind on this shift. In some sense this is surprising, because AutoML has unusual potential to facilitate ‘beyond human AI’. For example, compared to typical supervised deep learning algorithms, AutoML algorithms can deal with much more complicated decision variables and objective functions that do not require a precise mathematical relation, making them much more flexible. This article makes a theoretical contribution by characterizing some of the ways in which AutoML could facilitate the creation of AI systems that go ‘beyond human’. First, it introduces AutoML and describes how the AutoML research community has recently investigated moving toward being human-centered in a particular sense. Next, the article describes how many other AI research communities, after moving toward human-centered AI in various senses in recent years, are now moving to consider the importance of ‘beyond human’ values. The article then turns to how AutoML research could possibly go ‘beyond human.’ Whereas many aspects of human-centered AutoML, such as transparency, may also advance ‘beyond human’ values, doing so in a reliable way would require moving beyond human-centered AutoML. The article then demonstrates that in comparison with typical supervised deep learning approaches, the flexibility of AutoML offers unique opportunities for facilitating ‘beyond human’ values that are not present in other areas of AI. If there is merit in developing systems that go beyond human values, as many people outside of AutoML seem to think, then AutoML offers a number of advantages.
items.title: Beyond human-centered automated machine learning
Consequence-bearing transition: a formal theory of when AI-generated transitions acquire authority to bind consequences
The algorithmic muhtasib: an islamic moral-economy architecture for accountable AI governance in the digital state

items.abstract: Abstract In the architectural design by Dominique Perrault of the fourth (2008) and fifth (2019) renovation and extension of the Courts of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) in Luxembourg, the lead colour is gold. This article poses the question: why gold? Or, more precisely, what is the architectural story told in gold? In approaching this question, the article draws on research about the physical architecture of courtrooms in socio-legal studies and joins in on the call to bring a spatial inquiry to the study of EU law. It thus engages with scholarship on law and architecture, design, materiality and notably colour. Concretely, the article proceeds by tracing two design narratives communicated by the Court itself: a historic reference to the European Community of Coal and Steel and a recurring reference to the classical Greek drama. It shows these two narratives as stories of origin and beginning, which ultimately position the Court at the centre of the EU project. The article argues that, whether seen as solemn and serene or as incredibly ‘bling’, this golden design amplifies pre-held views of the CJEU.
items.title: ‘If the law were a colour [it would be gold]’: the architecture of the CJEU

items.abstract: Abstract Ben Judah’s This is Europe brings into view the everyday lives lived in Europe today, often marked by inequalities, exclusion and alienation. It therefore forms a useful starting point from which to reflect on the emerging ‘European society’ discourse in the EU legal discipline. Presenting EU law as being grounded in a society founded on shared values, EU institutions and scholars legitimise far-reaching legal and political innovations, but do not account for the plurality of values and lived experiences on the ground. By taking these as a starting point, This is Europe offers a means to think about the role of EU law and legal scholarship unaffected by an institutional gaze.
items.title: Confronting European Society with the Everyday

items.abstract: Abstract This article relies on Ben Judah’s This is Europe for a conceptual intervention into how European law is seen, narrated and normatively assessed. It analyses European law as a mode of social risk allocation embedded in the normativity of everyday life through four connected lenses: social structures, risk, individuation and resilience. First, Judah’s testimonies reveal that everyday life in Europe is shaped by social structures that enable or constrain agency, generate vulnerability to injustice and influence how injustice itself is perceived. Second, European law – both through regulation and through its omission – is deeply implicated in these structures. It is a key mode of societal organisation as it allocates social risk across a plurality of actors, institutions and networks. Third, the article argues that, since the late twentieth century, European law has increasingly shifted social risks and responsibility for social inclusion onto individuals, a process I call individuation. Individuation leaves each person alone to navigate social structures while obscuring the responsibility of public and collective institutions for mediating them and their injustices. Fourth, the article proposes a different way of seeing Europe’s law of the everyday : as a framework for resilience , centred on risk allocation. Resilience here does not mean conservation or mere adaptation to injustice without structural change. Instead, it refers to a transformative idea: to reflect on the organisation of society via risk-sharing, with the aim being that social structures interact with law in order to prevent, contain and mitigate injustice and support a more habitable society and planet. On this account, the central question of legal ordering is not whether risk is allocated, but how.
items.title: Ways of seeing European law anew: Structures, risk, individuation and resilience

items.abstract: Abstract Although AI can accelerate scientific discovery, it also generates new epistemic risks that prevailing rule-based governance frameworks are structurally ill-equipped to address. We present four arguments for the claim that intellectual virtues offer an adequate response to the challenges of AI-accelerated science. The Adaptability Argument states that rules cannot keep pace with technological change. The Motivation Gap Argument shows that compliance does not amount to epistemic motivation. The Human-in-the-Loop Argument stresses that AI systems require virtuous human interpretation. Finally, the Fallibility-in-Principle Argument maintains that AI systems remain fallible and, therefore, require human oversight. Moreover, we develop the first systematic mapping of intellectual virtues onto the CRediT (contributor roles taxonomy) stages of the research process and extend this to encompass the process of scientific evaluation. In doing so, we bridge virtue epistemology and the governance of AI-accelerated science. We show how virtues such as intellectual justice, intellectual scrutiny, intellectual humility, curiosity, and intellectual courage constitute the intellectual infrastructure that enables scientists to evaluate AI-generated outputs and preserve epistemic agency in an era of increasing outsourcing of cognitive effort. This virtue-based framework offers a proactive and future-oriented normative foundation for scientific practice in the age of AI.
items.title: Navigating AI-Accelerated Science: An Intellectual Virtue Approach to Responsible Inquiry

items.abstract: Abstract Misogyny is traditionally understood as hatred against women. Contra this view, Kate Manne (2018) argued that “misogyny” should be defined as a sanction-distributing mechanism that punishes women who violate gender norms and rewards women who comply with them. Here, I argue for a novel approach in characterising “misogyny.” The paper consists of two main parts. In the negative one, I acknowledge the deficiencies of both accounts. Specifically, I focus on the limitations of Manne’s definition. First, I argue that Manne’s reactive reading of misogyny downplays her account’s predictive capacity and aspired extensional scope. Second, I propose that the affective dimension should be given more prominence. Then, I outline the desiderata for an adequate account of “misogyny.” The suggested approach is to integrate the psychological and structural perspectives by (i) incorporating the structural explanation of the phenomenon by definition, and (ii) treating the affective dimension as a core part of misogyny.
items.title: A Novel Approach in Characterising Misogyny
Review of Catala’s The Dynamics of Epistemic Injustice

items.abstract: Abstract The “Founding” is a keyword in the United States’ constitutional vocabulary. Across popular politics, public law, and civic culture, it signifies a closed moment of constitutional creation—and often much more. Invocations commonly involve vague yet powerful significations about constitutional authority, memory, and meaning-making. Particularly as “originalist” judicial and academic writing leans on these submerged qualities, it is worth asking: what is the Founding? This Article proposes a conceptual answer in historical context. Through a close study of contours of antebellum constitutionalism, it argues for understanding the Founding as an ideology that committed Americans to venerate and defer to an authoritative, originary constitutional era. Forged as citizens grappled with the politics of slavery, the Founding structured language and perception, motivated action and inaction, and delimited boundaries of political possibility. This Article studies two essential sites of inculcation apart from formal power—civic ceremonies and educational practices—to sketch the structure of the constitutional Founding as ideology. Then, it outlines how that ideology authorized constitutional actions of voting, legislating, judging, protesting, and seceding. In conclusion, the Article suggests that its analysis models a broader framework for interpreting the diffuse materials of constitutional life across periodizations of constitutional history. Approaching the Founding as ideology can allow scholars to better see how its relative authority over time and the purposes to which it has been directed have shaped American constitutional experience.
items.title: The Founding as Ideology

Faisal Chaudhry , South Asia, The British Empire, and the Rise of Classical Legal Thought: Towards a Historical Ontology of the Law, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2024. Pp. 560. £130.00 hardback (ISBN 9780198916482)
In defense of rethinking metaphysics
Against the interaction theory of metaphor

items.abstract: Abstract Anscombe’s 1947 report to the Mary Somerville Fellowship Committee shows that she had engaged with some (then) contemporary empirical work on psychokinesis—parapsychological research that Wittgenstein was also aware of. I first show that this critical engagement shaped her treatment of action in Intention. Human intentional action is essentially ‘at a distance’ or at scale. I then advance a fresh take on Anscombean practical knowledge by analogy with prophecy.
items.title: Anscombe and the ‘Reach’ of the Mind

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Using a psychoanalytic lens attuned to preoedipal phenomena, this article argues that neoliberal precarity produces and exacerbates conditions that draw people to fascism. This article shows how neoliberalism produces annihilation anxieties and conditions on which fascism feeds. With mounting anxieties and scant collective means for dealing with them, people easily succumb to fascism's promise of a life raft and safe harbor in precarious times. At bottom, the essence of fascism is its logic for appeasing unconscious demands for ways to ward off debilitating, politically produced anxieties. This logic leads to three overarching fascist delusions: bending reality; a mythic past; and eliminationism. This analysis provides a way to see fascism's deep structure as a palliative that allows a world out of joint continue to be so.
items.title: Authoritarianism's Annihilation Anxieties

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Inferentialism faces two influential objections: (i) it is not compositional and (ii) there is a lack of fruitful application of inferentialism to problems in philosophy of language and formal semantics. In this paper, I defend inferentialism against both charges. In particular, I do so by focusing on a central problem in philosophy of language and formal semantics—the problem(s) of anaphora licensing. I show that, by developing a compositional version of inferentialism, inferentialism can give more satisfactory solutions to the problem(s) of anaphora licensing compared to rival truth‐conditional theories.
items.title: Inferentialism, Compositionality, and Anaphora

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article discusses prize‐creation and prize‐allocation. Such activities may seem morally neutral, or perhaps even beneficial. A central thesis of this article is that such practices have significant moral implications and should be brought under the remit of moral reasoning. I suggest that in many cases, the harmful effects of prizes are overlooked, and that they stand in need of scrutiny, revision, and possibly abolition. This conclusion is reached via an examination of the nature of prizes, their functions, benefits, and harms, which generates guidelines that prize‐giving institutions should consider before instituting prizes and should use to periodically review them. This article advances philosophical theorising about prizes and has significant practical upshots.
items.title: On Prizes
No Justice, No Peace: The Ethics of Violent Protests. A.Pasternak, 2025. Oxford, Oxford University Press. 288 pp, £22.99 (hb)
Governing Fairness in Insurance Pricing: The Trilemma of Actuarial Adequacy, Solidarity, and Causal Legitimacy

items.abstract: Abstract Improvements in large language model (LLM) capability can increase accuracy, reasoning, and access to relevant information while leaving unassessed whether a particular output is appropriately presented for epistemic uptake. This creates an evaluative gap: first-order capability metrics can register genuine gains while leaving claim-presentation conditions underdetermined. LLM outputs increasingly occupy assertion-like roles without thereby acquiring the standing of accountable asserters. We develop assertability as a relational normative status of an output-in-practice, determined by the evidential and contextual conditions governing its presentation. One such condition is the evidence frame: the set of sources admissible as grounds within an interaction. A true answer, or one well supported outside the governing frame, may therefore remain non-assertable when it relies on an inadmissible evidential basis. To address this capability–assertability gap, we use epistemic regulation to denote the normative-functional regulation of whether and how an LLM-mediated output is presented for epistemic uptake in light of the conditions bearing on its assertability. We organize the framework across four regulatory loci—assertoric force, evidential grounding, evidential candor, and epistemic response selection. The framework is normative-functional, while its realization may be distributed across learned behavior, retrieval and verification mechanisms, interface design, evaluation, deployment rules, and institutional practices, with responsibility and accountability remaining with identifiable human and organizational actors. Because standards governing assertion, qualification, verification, and withholding can distribute epistemic risk and verification burdens unevenly, their specification and oversight are also governance questions rather than merely technical calibration choices.
items.title: From capability to assertability: epistemic regulation of LLM-mediated claim presentation

items.abstract: Abstract This paper sets out to defend the intellectual potential of a relational view of speech by considering the nature, value, and limits of free speech in a domain in which it is seldom examined: social institutions. The latter consist of work organisations, universities, churches, political parties, trade unions, campaign groups, charities, sports teams, and so on. The paper’s argument sits on two pillars. First, I contend that institutions consist of interlocking roles, orientated by an over-arching institutional purpose. Those roles consist inter alia of social norms, including rights and obligations, which have a deontic character and enable mutual accountability. Second, I defend a relational view of speech centred on our need to be recognised, by our interlocutor, as a participant in discursive practices in good standing, where each person also recognises others through their speech. With those in mind, the paper’s core argument is that speech within institutions recognises and makes real the constituent roles of those institutions, including their attendant normative demands. Indeed, much institutional speech involves, precisely, the exercise of institutionally defined rights, obligations, and other norms to which members may hold one another to account. Speech which fails to respect institutional norms, rights and duties, and, in particular, which undermines an institution’s purpose, may legitimately be subject to sanction. The latter decentres the doctrine of viewpoint neutrality, usually seen as essential to free speech.
items.title: Institutional Speech: Social Norms and Social Roles

items.abstract: Abstract Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are behavioral programs, often involving practices like meditation, that aim to cultivate mindfulness , the nonjudgmental awareness of present-moment experience. A growing body of evidence suggests that they are effective for treating a range of physical and mental health conditions. Critics, however, argue that much of this evidence is biased, relying heavily on uncontrolled or poorly controlled studies, and is therefore insufficient to warrant the widespread clinical adoption of MBIs. More randomized controlled trials (RCTs)—widely regarded as the “gold standard” of scientific evidence—are needed (Van Dam et al., 2018). In this paper, I argue that, although RCT study design has several advantages, it also embodies reductionistic assumptions about how and why an intervention produces its effects. In particular, it assumes that such effects can be attributed to a single, isolable “active ingredient.” In contrast, the features of MBIs, including the attitudes and forms of effort they require, are not readily decomposable into “ingredients.” Moreover, a prominent attempt to isolate mindfulness as an active ingredient (MacCoon et al., 2012) ultimately does not succeed. I conclude that RCTs should not be treated as the gold standard of evidence for MBIs or other complex behavioral interventions for which these assumptions may not hold. Doing so undermines the value of evidence for nonreductionistic hypotheses about how they function and risks underestimating their effectiveness.
items.title: Are randomized controlled trials the “gold standard” of evidence for mindfulness-based interventions?
Mitigating power imbalance and epistemic asymmetry: a phenomenological model of attitude-switching in shared decision-making
The Dynamics of Analogical Arguments and Their Evaluation

items.abstract: Abstract As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly infused in religious communication from generative sermon-writing tools to avatar-led worship services, religious organizations are emerging as important yet underexamined sites of AI leadership and governance. Existing responsible AI scholarship has focused primarily on corporate and governmental settings, leaving limited understanding of how AI practices are ethically negotiated within civil society and faith-based institutions. Addressing this gap, this article examines how Christian religious organizations understand, evaluate, and govern the integration of AI within their digital media environments. Empirically, the study analyzes AI developments in three case studies involving 66 leaders from religious organizations in the United States, Germany and Switzerland. The findings identify three interrelated modes of normative, collaborative, and experimentative adaptivity through which religious leaders navigate the opportunities, risks, and uncertainties of emerging AI technologies. Building on these insights, we advance value-based adaptive governance as a framework for understanding how religious institutions function as learning organizations that actively influence AI development through theology-informed ethical assessment and participatory practices. Responding to calls for more relational and action-oriented AI ethics research, this article contributes to AI ethics by foregrounding religion as a distinctive organizational and cultural domain, demonstrating how Christian values, theological reflection, and institutional mission shape ethical reasoning, authority, cross-scalar collaboration, and spiritual discernment in human-centered AI governance.
items.title: Artificial intelligence, religion, and society: ethical leadership and the shaping of value-based adaptive governance
Mal-Intelligence: how artificial intelligence produces a sustained illusion of cognitive competence

items.abstract: Abstract Legal comparatists have attempted to conceptually grasp the traveling of laws since the field’s institutional inception. Tellingly, one finds ubiquitously undergirding such intellectual efforts—and the resistance thereto—a range of what Hans Blumenberg has once dubbed as “background metaphors,” such as: transplants, grafting, cross-fertilization, migration, translation, reception, transfer, among others. There is not a single investigation on the subject matter pursued under the auspices of metaphorology. This contribution addresses this gap. Harkening back to Blumenberg’s proposal, whose fundamental appreciation underscores the fact that metaphors carry a history in a more radical sense than concepts, but also harvesting from the embrace and revisitation of Blumenberg’s claims by the literature on cultural techniques, this argument focuses on the metaphor of traveling laws. As it explores how the curve of this metaphor’s history provides us with key insights into the radical multiplicity of laws and their movement, it grounds this excavatory enterprise in a concrete undertaking: the pursuit of a case study concerning the traveling of environmental laws between Brazil and Germany.
items.title: Traveling Laws: On Comparison-at-Law’s Metaphors and Cultural Techniques

The Criminal Record Complex: Risk, Race, and the Struggle for Work in America

items.abstract: Abstract Descartes’s account of generosity, his alternative to magnanimity, is the richest source of his thought on how individuals should interact with others. In response to recent scholarship emphasizing the beneficence of the generous person, I argue that this beneficence is best understood in terms of the awareness of self-sufficiency core to generosity. Understanding generosity as a universally available awareness of one’s own freedom as the highest good explains the egalitarian judgments made by the generous person and her resulting beneficence. Exploring generous pity, veneration, and gratitude reveals that the generous person is alienated from others, and analyzing Descartes’s self-presentation in Discourse VI shows the importance of isolation to beneficence. This suggests that Descartes does not view relationships as key to human flourishing, and moreover that scholars who describe generosity in terms of love and friendship should note that these concepts are austere and depersonalized in the case of the generous individual.
items.title: Descartes’s Generosity: Self-Sufficiency as Ideal Sociability
The first right: self-determination and the transformation of international order, 1941–2000

items.abstract: Abstract As Clinical Ethics Consultation (CEC) becomes more institutionalized, concerns about its legitimacy and efficacy have grown. We defend a realist orientation, according to which CEC has normative force only if its recommendations answer to stance-independent reasons, not to individual preferences and institutional policies. Public justification can and should proceed through familiar means (e.g., shared mid-level norms and transparent procedures) so that stakeholders can scrutinize the reasoning. We show how neutrality, admirable as a procedural virtue, hollows CEC when treated as a master ideal, leaving hard cases to defaults and institutional inertia. In its place, we develop moral expertise as sustained, transparent reasoning that integrates the clinical picture with the profession’s content-full standards. We then construe warranted deference as rational trust in contrastive reason-tracking rather than deference to role. Our comparative thesis holds that shared norms successfully handle routine cases, but persistent disagreement and institutional pressure call for a realist grounding that secures determinate, action-guiding recommendations. On such realist understanding, CEC remains normatively accountable and oriented toward getting things right.
items.journal: The Journal of Medicine and Philosophy: A Forum for Bioethics and Philosophy of Medicine
items.title:
Clinical

                    in Name Only? The Case for Moral Realism at the Bedside

items.abstract: Abstract We provide an argument for the thesis that there could not have been nothing, given that there is something. Only one non-logical assumption goes into our argument. The assumption in question is supported by intuitive considerations as well as by three currently popular views about metaphysical modality. Moreover, our argument can be proven to be valid in the weak modal system K. If a posteriori assumptions are permitted, then the argument can be extended into an argument for why there could not have been nothing, period. The extended argument avoids the controversial assumptions made by previous attempts to establish the same thesis.
items.title: Nothing is impossible, actually

items.abstract: ABSTRACT In the 1920s and 1930s, Walter Benjamin and Theodor W. Adorno both sought to develop a notion of Darstellung —of philosophical presentation or representation—that could provide an alternative to the classically idealist tendency to subsume objects under abstract concepts. Benjamin's influence on Adorno is therefore often narrativized through the latter's early work, in which Adorno appears as Benjamin's “disciple” in the 1930s before later developing an independent philosophical voice. I seek to complicate this narrative through an investigation of the term “constellation,” which appears prominently in Benjamin's work before being repurposed by Adorno. The constellation first surfaces in the “Epistemo‐Critical Foreword” to Origin of the German Trauerspiel , where it combines with a host of other key terms to depict Benjamin's early notion of Darstellung . In “The Actuality of Philosophy,” Adorno reconfigures the constellation to outline his own conception of interpretive philosophy. While this might initially appear to support the narrative of discipleship, it is argued that Adorno's reconception becomes distinct once the constellation is isolated from the structure of terms laid out by Benjamin. In particular, Adorno places greater emphasis on the interpretive subject, reflecting early reservations about what he would later characterize as Benjamin's “anti‐subjectivism.” At the same time, Benjamin's resistance to Hegelian mediation reflects a concern to preserve the primacy of the object against idealist conceptual domination. Adorno's enduring use of the constellation thus reflects the dialectic of differentiation and appropriation through which he attempts to synthesize Benjamin's object‐focused methodology with his own emphasis on subjective mediation and Hegelian dialectics.
items.title: The Constellation: A Reappraisal of Walter Benjamin's Influence on Theodor W. Adorno
The Cosmopolitan Tradition: A Noble but Flawed Ideal, written by Martha Nussbaum

items.abstract: Abstract Modern states increasingly use AI systems in public decision-making, including benefits eligibility, risk classification, immigration adjudication, and judicial administration. Defenders often argue that democratic authorization, validation, and review are sufficient to render such systems legitimate; critics often reply that human beings must decide. I argue that both responses miss a deeper question: what distinguishes a lawful procedure from a publicly imputable judgment? Drawing on Kant’s Rechtslehre , I argue that when the state makes a materially burdensome, legally operative, reasonably contestable, and practically final determination of a person’s legal status, the legally operative ground of that determination must be attributable to an answerable office with the authority, capacity, and institutional independence to adopt or reject it as its own. This yields a right to an answer: a right to be governed through office-owned judgment rather than unowned architecture. The argument does not condemn AI in public administration. It identifies the moral threshold at which algorithmic assistance becomes impermissible substitution.
items.title: Office and unowned architecture: public judgment in the age of algorithmic governance
Neuropanopticon and the Self-as-Platform: Neurotechnologies as Power Tools in the Workplace
David Clowney: Environmental Ethics and our Collective Character

items.abstract: Abstract The relevance of empirical studies on intuitions to normative theorising remains contested. This paper proposes a framework to structure the debate. It argues that empirical studies on intuitions should be classified according to which features of intuitions they illuminate: aetiology, function, robustness, universality, and substance. It also proposes general and specific approaches to advance the discussion. The paper then applies the framework to the moral luck debate. First, it considers how empirical studies regarding intuitions’ aetiology and function can impact our method of relying on intuitions. Next, it illustrates how studies on the aetiology and function of the causation intuition may reshape the moral luck debate by weakening the intuitive challenge to the control intuition. In so doing, it demonstrates how empirical studies on intuitions can have significant implications for normative disputes more generally.
items.title: Normative Theorising and Empirical Studies on Intuitions: A Case Study on Moral Luck
Polylaminin, Evidence, and Emotion: When Hope Outpaces Science
Knowledge-how and Gettier-cases

items.abstract: Abstract Extant dual character concept theories hold that utterances like `\textit{a} is not a scientist but, ultimately, \textit{a} is a true scientist' are felicitous because the head noun is polysemous, denoting a concept that permits dissociated categorization along descriptive and normative lines. This paper develops an eliminativist critique of such theories, arguing that this sort of dissociation is incoherent on a literal reading and requires pragmatic reinterpretation to achieve felicity at the level of speaker meaning. If such utterances are indeed coherent in context, they are more plausibly explained by context-sensitive category extension than by the hybrid lexical structures posited by dual character theories. Thus, eliminativism dispenses with dual character concepts and offers a semantically parsimonious treatment of double dissociation, {emphasizing} the importance of distinguishing between literal and loose categorization.
items.title: Dual Character Eliminativism

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article argues that existential risk is not only a threat to welfare or survival, but also a problem for political freedom. It begins with gene‐length nucleic‐acid synthesis, a socially valuable technology whose misuse could contribute to catastrophic biological risk. Harm‐based views explain why such risks matter, and negative‐liberty views explain why regulation may burden researchers and firms. Yet both miss the standing dependence that arises when publics must rely on the restraint, competence, and secrecy practices of actors whose catastrophic capabilities they cannot meaningfully control. Republican theory identifies this condition as domination. The article develops survivable freedom, the claim that under sufficiently high, agent‐mediated existential vulnerability, a durable baseline of collective survival is constitutive of robust non‐domination rather than a merely external precondition of liberty. The claim is conditional and empirically modest. It applies where catastrophic leverage is agent‐mediated, structurally persistent, institutionally reducible, and insufficiently contestable. The article then sketches republican capability governance through ex ante controls, public authorization, democratic contestation, auditable expertise, legally governed secrecy, review, and remedy. Such governance seeks neither libertarian complacency nor unchecked guardianship, but survival‐oriented institutions constrained by non‐domination.
items.title: Survivable Freedom: Republican Non‐Domination under Existential Vulnerability

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Limitarianism's paramount claim is that no one should possess surplus wealth. Ingrid Robeyns's Power of Material Resources (PMR), the leading operationalization of that claim, identifies such surplus through a snapshot of income and annuitized assets. This article argues that the PMR is self‐defeating. It does not punish the appropriation of excessive resources, but only their retention: it thereby penalizes individuals who save while privileging those with identical inflows who immediately consume away their surplus before it can be recorded against the limitarian threshold. Limitarianism therefore does more than fail to prevent waste: it can incentivize it – a result incompatible with Robeyns's own non‐intrinsic justifications, which rely on harnessing morally weightless surplus wealth to address urgent needs. As a corrective, this article proposes a lifetime limitarianism , operating under a lifetime PMR (L‐PMR), which caps total resource appropriation over a lifespan regardless of usage. Under the L‐PMR, prudence is no longer punished, and profligacy is no longer privileged.
items.title: The Profligacy Paradox: Why Limitarianism Needs a Lifetime Limit
What Becomes of Kinematics and Dynamics When Spacetime Goes Missing?

items.abstract: Abstract Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) is expected to become a core capability of future 6G networks, enabling wireless infrastructures to sense physical environments and human presence through shared radio resources. While offering significant technological benefits, ISAC also raises ethical and societal concerns due to its invisible and pervasive sensing nature. This paper proposes a human-centric, questionnaire-based framework to assess the acceptability of ISAC functionalities and to operationalize ethical and societal perceptions into quantitative, design-oriented indicators. Two representative human-centric scenarios are investigated, namely domestic monitoring for Ambient Assisted Living and human motion monitoring for safety. The proposed framework directly quantifies selected 6G human-centric values, including trustworthiness and regulation, and identifies additional design requirements related to transparency, user control, and system understanding that significantly influence acceptability. The results show that ISAC acceptance is strongly context-dependent and driven more by governance, trust, and knowledge than by sensing capabilities alone. By translating user perceptions into actionable indicators and design requirements, this work provides a practical contribution toward ethical-by-design ISAC development, complementing traditional performance metrics and supporting the realization of transparent, trustworthy, and socially acceptable 6G networks.
items.title: When networks sense and decide: a preliminary investigation of the human and invisible ethical dimensions of ISAC in 6G

items.abstract: Abstract This special issue focuses on forms of resistance to dominant development discourses and practices in Latin America. The attention is on the processes and practices through which grassroot groups challenge the capacity of official legal orders to recognise and address their concerns and demands. These groups have different names in the literature: ‘social movements’, ‘frontier communities’, ‘the oppressed’, ‘political society’, ‘uncivil civil society’, and others. The aim of this special issue is to move beyond certain common approaches in critical literature, which either unwillingly ignores these groups’ agency and portrays them as mere victims, thus infantilising their experience and diminishing their agency, or bestows upon them heroic features as ‘social movements’, thus creating a high threshold of political and theoretical relevance that only few movements with global visibility can meet.
items.title: Resisting ‘Nice Development’ in Latin America

items.abstract: Abstract Resistance to development projects that inflict harm upon local communities and destroy their livelihoods and ways of life has become increasingly difficult as development is getting cloaked in green and sustainability guises, while financial structures prioritise timely repayment and investors’ interests. This article explores the role of law in financialised development, specifically in reshaping communities and territories to suit project needs, and how grassroots' everyday practices resist law’s representations and violence. We do it through the lens of Rios Vivos’ opposition to Hidroituango, Colombia’s largest hydroelectric dam. Rios Vivos is a network of grassroot organizations of peoples affected and threatened by dams, diversions, and projects alike. They have opposed Hidroituango since 2010, resorting to a diverse repertoire of contention, ranging from protests to international litigation. We pay close attention to how Ríos Vivos depicts their everyday life in digital spaces such as their website and YouTube channel. We argue that, beyond contesting narratives of backwardness, poverty, and environmental degradation that justify their sacrifice in the face of the project, Rios Vivos emphasis on everyday practices reveals how, through everyday care and work, communitarian politics grounded on care and solidarity can emerge. These practices carve out spaces for alternative social configurations that transcend the logics of development and accumulation.
items.title: Everyday resistance against green financialised development: an example of Rios Vivos resisting Hidroituango in Colombia
Toward a Refined Account of Argumentative Injustice: The Role of ad hominem Argument and Emotion
Contagion, Technology, and Law at the Limits
Celebrating women in legal history: making and shaping a discipline

items.abstract: In Europe, open GLAM movements and cultural restitution reforms are overlooking a crucial aspect that should not be underestimated: what should happen to the archival materials, digital collections and intellectual property that are indelibly linked to cultural property. Left unresolved, new inequities will emerge around who can own, access, use, control and commercialise the heritage for decades. The effect is to conflate layers of discrete rights in the underlying item and knowledge it contains, securing to possessors a double monopoly over the digital and physical heritage. To redress this in both practice and legal reforms, this article argues that the focus on restitution must expand from one on cultural property to one on intellectual property to include a wider range of heritage assets. Given that these materials largely fall within private law, this means the possessor's ability to return such heritage is not dependent on public law reform; restitution can begin now.
items.title: Intellectual Property Restitution
Cosmic Connections: Poetry in the Age of Disenchantment. By Charles Taylor, Harvard University Press, 2024. 640 pp., $37.95 (hbk). ISBN: 9780674296084

items.abstract: ABSTRACT There is no precise characterization of the A‐ and B‐theories that has won a consensus in the literature. In this paper, we set out to provide clear formulations of these theories in the setting of higher‐order logic in what we call the operational framework . In the operational framework, the disagreement between the A‐ and B‐theories centers on the distribution of accuracy among times. We will show that these formulations of the A‐ and B‐theories produce strong predictions about various features of temporal reality. We will address some objections that could be made to the operational framework from both A‐ and B‐theorists. We will also examine how the operational framework helps us think about the ideological commitments of the A‐ and B‐theories. We will close by suggesting ways in which this framework can be applied to other topics in the metaphysics of temporal intervals, spacetime, modality, and first‐person perspectives.
items.title: A Theory of the A‐Theory

items.abstract: Abstract Despite the growing importance of entrepreneurship as a pathway to economic mobility, ethnic minority entrepreneurs continue to face persistent disadvantages in access to capital, particularly following business failure. This study examines how ethnic stereotypes and evaluators’ ethnic identity shape perceptions of funding-worthiness for Latinx entrepreneurs relative to White non-Latinx entrepreneurs in the United States. Using a full-profile conjoint experiment comprising 12,496 evaluations from 781 evaluators, we provide evidence of systematic ethnicity-based disparities in post-failure funding assessments. Latinx entrepreneurs are evaluated as less funding-worthy than White entrepreneurs, even when objective financial indicators such as the level of debt indicate comparable or lower financial risk. These findings suggest that favorable financial attributes do not fully offset ethnicity-based disadvantages in evaluations. We further show that the ethnic identity of evaluators conditions these evaluations. Shared ethnic identity does not mitigate ethnicity-based disparities in perceived funding-worthiness. Instead, Latinx evaluators evaluate Latinx entrepreneurs less favorably than White evaluators. Together, these findings show how post-failure funding evaluations are shaped by embedded ethnic hierarchies, reproducing inequality in entrepreneurial finance. By identifying how ethnic stereotypes and ethnic identity jointly influence funding assessments, this study advances research on ethnic minority entrepreneurship and contributes to business ethics scholarship by clarifying mechanisms through which systemic inequality is sustained in evaluative decision-making.
items.title: The Effect of Ethnic Stereotypes and Evaluators’ Ethnic Identity on Funding-Worthiness: Evidence About Latinx Entrepreneurs in the United States

items.abstract: Abstract This study examines how age-based exclusion is materially organized, discursively justified, and experienced within everyday commercial environments. Drawing on marketing systems theory and critical spatial theory, it conceptualizes commercial space as moral infrastructure through which market participation is organized. Using topic modeling of public discourse and in-depth interviews with older consumers, the study examines the discursive, material, and lived dimensions of age-based exclusion. Public discourse legitimates exclusion through five recurring justificatory themes: moral generalization, economic rationalization, youth-centered normalization, behavioral stigmatization, and institutional normalization. Interview accounts illustrate how material and operational arrangements, including kiosks, service practices, and youth-oriented spatial design, can shape older consumers’ participation and how participants experience and negotiate these conditions through discomfort, anticipatory withdrawal, behavioral self-regulation, and the internalization of market expectations. The findings suggest a spatial mechanism through which public discourse can legitimate exclusion, material arrangements can organize participation, and lived experience can shape expectations of belonging and non-belonging. The study contributes to business ethics by showing how age-based exclusion can be understood as a form of structural injustice reproduced through routine market coordination within marketing systems.
items.title: Spatializing Ageism in Commercial Spaces: Discursive Justifications and Lived Experiences of Age-Based Exclusion
Publisher Correction: Eliminating Idealizations with Soundness Analysis
Oral Voting with a Balanced Procedure

items.abstract: Abstract One pressing concern in the world at the moment concerns the gathering and use of personal information in digital contexts. This may be one of the main reasons why so much of the recent literature on the philosophy of privacy focuses on ‘informational privacy’—that which can be explained in terms of information about a person, instead of something like the privacy of a particular location : a bedroom, a lockbox, etc. This paper argues that narrowing the focus in this way has led to some important mistakes about how privacy can be diminished. It is important to remember that there is rarely an easy or clear delineation between informational and locational privacy. In particular, I argue that this wider perspective allows us to see differences in how we treat information—privacy over one’s information is still diminished when that privacy is ‘invaded’ or ‘intruded upon’, regardless of the mental states of the invader. This has both practical upshots in the ethics of mass surveillance by non-humans, and theoretical upshots in the debates about the theoretical nature of privacy itself.
items.title: Types of Privacy: On the Distinction between Locational and Informational
Beyond Separability: Closed-Loop Brain Stimulation and the Distribution of Moral Responsibility
Care for the Caregivers: Ethical Responsibilities to Caregivers in BCI Research
From false attribution to synthetic personation: personational integrity and a residual tort for deepfake harms
AI-assisted retrospective reconstruction of contested psychiatric care: an autoethnographic case study

items.abstract: Abstract This paper argues for three main claims: (i) belonging can play an important role for epistemic self-trust; (ii) epistemic self-trust can be construed plurally so as to include not only its intellectual or propositional dimensions but also its experiential (practical, tacit, embodied, and affective) dimensions; and (iii) self-trust, plurally construed, can serve as a mechanism of epistemic repair to counteract various forms of epistemic injustice that undermine epistemic agency along these propositional and experiential dimensions. To make this threefold argument, I turn to the context of neurodiversity and neuronormativity, which helpfully illustrates the plural dimensions of epistemic agency, epistemic self-trust, and epistemic repair.
items.title: Belonging, Self-Trust, and Epistemic Repair

items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines whether relational autonomy can serve as a plausible ideal for postcolonial women despite persistent critiques that autonomy functions as a vehicle of liberal imperialism. It aims to reconstruct relational autonomy in a way that disrupts the epistemic hierarchy between Anglo-European and postcolonial contexts. To this end, it introduces the “axis of imperial imposition,” an analytical dimension that assesses how liberal-imperialist institutions condition the formation of volitional commitments and the exercise of agency in contexts where liberal normative frameworks are encountered through foreign imposition. Through the hypothetical case of “Western-oriented woman,” the paper argues that internalist accounts, which address epistemic hierarchy primarily through individual authenticity, are insufficient for this axis. It instead defends dialogical accounts that shift the focus to dialogical reflexivity and answerability, showing how postcolonial women can retain autonomy through local justificatory dialogue grounded in concrete socio-historical contexts. The paper further argues that self-regard in “creative appropriation”—the competence to reconfigure life-constructing materials from one’s situated knowledge—is necessary for the proper functioning of such dialogue. It concludes that postcolonial women’s autonomy is secured not by passively adopting liberal normative frameworks as universal standards but by actively reconfiguring them through locally grounded justificatory practices.
items.title: Is Relational Autonomy a Plausible Ideal for Postcolonial Women?

Turning Defenders into Defendants: The Use of Lawfare against Environmental Activists in Southeast Asia
                    . By Agung Wardana. Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2026.

items.abstract: Abstract The traditional analysis of a priori warrant is negative: warrant for a belief is a priori just in case it does not depend on experience. To ward off obvious counterexamples, a standard exemption is made for learning experiences. In order to believe that the square root of two is irrational, I first needed to learn the relevant concepts, and this happened through experience. This standard exemption is not enough. I formed my warranted belief about the square root of two by reading the proof in Euclid’s Elements . This experience isn’t covered by the standard exemption, so the traditional analysis counts even basic mathematical beliefs as a posteriori . This is a disaster, but it can be fixed. The fix involves an ‘imagination test’ for determining which experiences are epistemically relevant and which are not. With the imagination test in hand, the negative approach may still provide the core of a satisfying analysis of the generative a priori , provided that various objections can be dealt with in a satisfying manner.
items.title:
Analyzing the
                    A Priori

Review -
                    Morality and Responsibility
                    by T. M. Scanlon, Polity Press, 2025, 272pp., £55 (hbk), ISBN: 9781509566969

Power and Possibility in Early Arabic Philosophy: Three Innovators between Philoponus and Avicenna
                    by Nicholas Allan Aubin, Scientia graeco-arabica 37, Walter de Gruyter, 2024, ix+286pp., €149,95 (hbk), ISBN 978-3-11-132492-0

How
                    Not
                    to Interpret the Constitution
Procedure, machines, and the transformation of American law: a review essay

items.abstract: Abstract The at-issue/not-at-issue distinction is based on a diverse collection of contrasts, both pragmatic and semantic. Providing a unified explanation of these contrasts remains an important open problem. In this paper, I show how the pragmatic differences between at-issue and not-at-issue content can be explained as the product of interlocutors’ strategic reasoning in response to their semantic differences. This explanation is first offered informally and then developed more formally within a game-theoretic setting using a modified version of the rejection game discussed in Sbardolini (2022) and Incurvati and Sbardolini (2024).
items.title: Strategic Content

items.abstract: Abstract This paper provides new examples of vagueness phenomena with comparatives. I show that comparatives of the form ‘x is ADJ-er than y’ can be vague due to a fuzziness in how much of some property makes for a difference in ADJ-ness. The sorites examples I provide cannot be assimilated to cases of indiscriminability or fuzziness in relevant dimensions, standards, or measurement procedures. A revised degree-based semantics with semiorders, a well-studied threshold structure, is developed. The treatment of equatives captures the truth of the claim that adjacent items in the sorites series are not relevantly distinguishable in ADJ-ness; and it avoids validating transitivities that would yield paradoxical conclusions.
items.title: Vagueness and the Comparative Form

items.abstract: Abstract My aim in this paper is to offer a novel justification for β-Equivalence. β-Equivalence is a standard principle of higher-order logic, but it is metaphysically controversial. My argument for β-Equivalence is based on a distinctively Fregean conception of predication. I argue that the Fregean conception motivates a non-standard notation for predicates, which can then be used to show that β-Equivalence is trivial on that conception. I also argue that the Fregean conception motivates a functional individuation of properties, which we can use to extend the Fregean justification for β-Equivalence to cover a more general principle, β-Conversion.
items.title: Fregean Predication

items.abstract: The Supreme Court in Re X and Y (Adoption Order: Setting Aside) confirms that there is no power under the High Court's inherent jurisdiction to set aside a properly made adoption order, even if the child's welfare would be better served by un‐doing the adoption. However, the importance of the case goes far beyond adoption, and raises challenging questions for the current renaissance that the inherent jurisdiction is experiencing, both in relation to children and in relation to incapacitous and so‐called ‘vulnerable’ adults. This note argues that Re X and Y represents the clearest modern articulation of constitutional limits on the High Court's inherent jurisdiction, and that a proper application of those limitations would significantly curtail other current uses of the inherent jurisdiction by the Family Division of the High Court. Important questions are raised about the constitutional appropriateness of the High Court's current uses of its inherent jurisdiction, including – as in Re X and Y – the extent to which that jurisdiction in fact exists.
items.title:
Limiting the High Court's Inherent Jurisdiction over Children:
                    Re X and Y (Adoption Order: Setting Aside)

items.journal: Free & Equal: A Journal of Ethics and Public Affairs
items.title: Temporal Partiality and the Veil of Ignorance

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Gossip is ubiquitous, yet morally troubling. Approximately 65% of human conversation involves evaluative talk about absent others, yet such talk often feels like backstabbing even when it causes no harm, violates no privacy, and consists entirely of truth. This article argues that gossip's distinctive wrong lies not in privacy violation, harm, or deception, but in something more fundamental which is the exclusion of targets from discourse about themselves. Building on this foundation, I develop three constraints on permissible gossip operating at different levels of moral analysis: participatory standing, purpose, and justice. These constraints together provide a framework for navigating gossip's complex moral terrain while respecting both the social value of information‐sharing and the dignity of those we discuss.
items.title: What Is Wrong with Gossip? An Exclusion‐Based Account

items.abstract: Abstract We respond to the comments by Imogen Dickie, Matthew Chrisman and Christine Tiefensee for a book symposium on our Reasoning with Attitude . Our commentators attempt to pull us further into either expressivism or into inferentialism. Here, we attempt to resist either pull and further establish our inferential expressivism as a home for both expressivists and inferentialists.
items.title: Replies to a fellow expressivist and two fellow inferentialists
Optimally tracking the truth: the ecological rationality of confirmation measures

items.abstract: Abstract Norms, rules, or standards require, recommend, or evaluate actions and attitudes. Claims about what agents have a reason to do or ought to do can be true according to or relative to standards. These statements will be familiar to anyone versed in recent work in metaethics and especially those interested in the debate over whether some standards are authoritatively as opposed to merely formally normative – i.e., the debate over whether some standards, like those of morality or prudence, ‘really’ or ‘genuinely’ tell agents what they have a reason to do or ought to do, while other standards, such as those which constitute certain conventional codes of behaviour, do not. But what are standards? And what is it for normative claims to be true or false according to standards? In this paper I raise a challenge for normative authority scepticism – the position that the idea that some standards are authoritatively normative is incoherent, confused, or otherwise defective – through an examination of these questions.
items.title: Standards and normative authority

items.abstract: Abstract AI ethics charters proliferate across the Arab world even as the same states deploy AI surveillance against domestic populations. The standard ethics-washing critique cannot diagnose this configuration because it was developed in democratic and corporate contexts and treats charter-implementation gaps as a single phenomenon. This paper introduces a Performative Authoritarianism Framework that draws the misfire and abuse distinction in Austin [1], pulls in the comparative-politics literature on authoritarian-upgrading, and operationalises the digital authoritarianism scholarship through a discursive scoping matrix. Five hypotheses are tested on the full N=22 cross-section of Arab League states using objective regulatory indicators, the AI Global Surveillance Index from Feldstein, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and a pre-specified test against the developmental-lag alternative. All five are supported, subject to the qualifications stated below. Of seven procedurally complete states (national strategy plus dedicated body), zero have enacted binding AI law. International ethics alignment co-occurs with documented AI surveillance deployment across the corpus (Spearman rho = 0.73, p < 0.001); the association is capacity-laden and does not reach significance within the institutionally capable subset, so the co-occurrence is reported as descriptive rather than as evidence of a sincere-commitment failure. Charter content covers consumer-protection domains at mean 0.90 of full coverage and regime-critical surveillance domains at 0.05 (Wilcoxon paired p = 0.008); this scoping gap is shared with democratic instruments coded on the same rubric, so the feature distinctive to the authoritarian corpus is the joint configuration of consumer-scoped principles, documented deployment in the excluded domains, and the absence of a binding backstop. State capacity is the strongest among several broadly necessary conditions for AI governance quality (fsQCA consistency = 0.91, ahead of regulatory maturity at 0.89, with five further conditions between 0.80 and 0.86, a margin that small recalibrations reverse); the ordering is read against collinearity among capacity-related conditions and is not presented as identifying a single dispositive cause. The developmental-lag alternative is not supported within the present cross-section: years since strategy adoption shows no positive association with substantive completion (rho = − 0.045), and the United Arab Emirates has had nine years post-strategy without enacting binding AI law. Pre-specified ex ante criteria are stated for the cases of Egypt and Bahrain that may transition out of the abuse configuration in the next 36 months. The abuse reading is advanced as the best-supported account of this configuration against the developmental-lag and sincere-prioritisation alternatives, not as a demonstrated property of regime intentions, and the framework identifies the institutional conditions under which the configuration is generated.
items.title: Performative authoritarianism in AI ethics charter production: a configurational analysis of 22 Arab states
Governance and accountability in compassionate AI: a normative framework for responsible design

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Although much ink has been spilled in discussing the relationship between rationality and normative reasons on the one hand and normative reasons and reasoning on the other, surprisingly little has been said about whether we can understand rationality in terms of reasoning. I propose a novel way to understand structural rationality in terms of good reasoning. I argue that structural rationality is best understood in terms of adherence to what I label indefeasible good reasoning. I then offer the beginnings of a theory of substantive rationality in terms of defeasible reasoning. I show how this can provide a unified account of structural and substantive dimensions of rationality, and show that my view also gives the right verdict in some challenging cases for other prominent theories.
items.journal: Journal of the American Philosophical Association
items.title: Reasoning, Rationality, and (In)Coherence

items.abstract: Abstract This essay’s core claim is that EU tech law does not fully understand technology, since it does not account for its diverse negative impacts in the everyday lives of people in European societies. Placing a central focus on EU’s digital regulation, I argue that EU law mostly sees technologies as products that should circulate at an ever-greater rate and volume in the internal market, to the benefit of consumers. This market-driven vision justifies a light-touch risk-based approach that creates a compliance apparatus which does not force tech companies to change unjust or harmful aspects of their business models; instead securing and legitimising them. Using a critical social theory approach, I argue that much of technology’s meaning and impact on the everyday lives of people is missed by EU law’s current depoliticised and technocratic approach to tech regulation. Taking the tech stories of This is Europe as a starting point, I illustrate how EU law systematically neglects the harms caused by technology or through technology to many individuals and communities in their everyday lives. Those affected range far beyond consumers and tech users. They include, for example, delivery platform workers forced into extreme anxiety due to task volume and app surveillance; several minorities systematically targeted by online abuse; or the migrants exposed to tech-mediated degrading treatment in European border facilities. All in all, EU law does not fully see, and therefore, epistemically excludes these lived experiences of tech harm from the regulatory dialogue. This leads me to some concluding reflections centred around a fundamental questioning of EU tech law’s legitimacy. Particularly, I argue that a legal regime that does not recognise and is not responsive to the lived realities of harm of those which it regulates ultimately fails at a deeper, politico-moral level.
items.title: People: What EU law does not understand about tech

items.abstract: Abstract What is it that is transmitted across known entailment from justified premises? My main aim in this paper is to clarify and defend the unpopular view that transmission of justification should be conceived as transmission of a justifier, and the search for cases in which transmission of justification fails should focus its energy on cases in which justifiers fail to be transmitted. The idea will take some time to develop, and along the way I will argue inter alia against Crispin Wright’s well-known account that it is a subtle kind of epistemic circularity that prevents some deductive arguments from transmitting the justification of their premises to their conclusions.
items.title: When Justifiers Transmit

items.abstract: Abstract Lex specialis derogat legi generali , the principle that special law prevails over general law, is a well-established doctrine for resolving conflicts between legal norms. Yet its application in fundamental rights adjudication remains underexplored. This Article contributes to this global discourse by examining the increasing invocation of this principle in Hong Kong courts. It scrutinizes the deployment of the principle in landmark cases: resolving the tension between indigenous inhabitants’ rights and the right to equality in Kwok Cheuk Kin v. Director of Lands ; balancing freedom of marriage against equality in Sham Tsz Kit v. Secretary for Justice ; and, as advanced by the Government, justifying the exclusion of married same-sex couples from public housing and inheritance entitlements in The Hong Kong Housing Authority v. Infinger, Nick and Secretary for Justice v. Li Yik Ho . Through a comparative jurisprudential analysis, this Article argues that the application in Kwok Cheuk Kin was legally sound, whereas its use in Sham Tsz Kit was problematic. Furthermore, it contends that where different constitutional instruments provide varying levels of protection for human rights, absent a clear legislative intent to the contrary, courts should uphold the higher standard of rights protection rather than relying on the lex specialis principle.
items.title:
The Use and Misuse of the
                    Lex Specialis
                    Principle in Hong Kong’s Fundamental Rights Adjudication

items.abstract: Abstract Accusations of over-sensitivity are common, particularly when it comes to forms of systemic oppression such as racism and misogyny. I consider three things such over-sensitivity could plausibly be: a disposition to over-identify instances of these phenomena, the over-expansion of the relevant concepts, and a tendency to overreact to putative instances thereof. In each case, I find reasons why such worries are likely to be overblown. In the first, an agent’s supposed over-sensitivity to racism and misogyny is often simply sensitivity to phenomena which are routinely minimized; in other cases, her slight over-sensitivity nevertheless has value in a social environment in which under-sensitivity is a large and predictable problem. In the second case, the supposed over-expansion of the relevant concepts often corrects for their artificial narrowing, and makes us more sensitive to genuine harms and wrongs. In the third case, an agent’s supposed overreactions to racism and misogyny reflects an affective disposition that constitutes a valuable defense against the twin perils of gaslighting and numbness. I conclude by considering the possibility that there is a real strand of over-sensitivity to harms to dominant group members in the current discourse that illicitly serves their interests and functions to silence people facing oppression.
items.title: Sensitivity and Survival
Kathryn Sophia Belle , Beauvoir and Belle: A Black Feminist Critique of The Second Sex

items.abstract: Abstract The litigation brought by the Estate of Henrietta Lacks against Thermo Fisher Scientific, Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical, and Novartis Pharmaceuticals reframes benefit-sharing from voluntary institutional ethics into an enforceable legal duty. By pleading a single equitable claim — unjust enrichment — the Estate seeks to bypass the property and informed-consent doctrines that have defeated comparable tissue-appropriation suits, while accepting distinctive risks involving remoteness, limitations, causation, and apportionment. This commentary examines the strategy’s strengths and vulnerabilities through the still-pending Ultragenyx case, and considers its implications for research consent, prospective benefit-sharing frameworks, and bioethics pedagogy. Whether or not the remaining claim succeeds, the litigation has already altered the conversation about who should profit from human biological materials.
items.title: The Henrietta Lacks Case: Ongoing Litigation Seeks Closure

items.abstract: In his final published essay, which appeared in the New York Review of Books shortly after his death in 1997, Isaiah Berlin reflected on the major themes of his life’s work. 1 Under the heading “Pluralism,” he wrote that “there is a plurality of values which men can and do seek, and … these values differ.” He argued that a belief in pluralism enables people to understand why others might endorse values different from their own. He also stressed that a belief in pluralism does not make one a relativist: “I do not say ‘I like my coffee with milk and you like it without; I am in favor of kindness and you prefer concentration camps.’” Pluralism as Berlin understands it is a key premise of Respect and Loathing in American Democracy. 2 Like Berlin, Spinner-Halev and Theiss-Morse believe there are plural values that people might endorse, including plural values that are reasonable in the Rawlsian sense that one can hold them while respecting others who do not. Examples are liberal values, such as individual liberty and human rights, and democratic values, such as popular sovereignty and political equality.
items.title: Pluralism vs. Moralism

items.abstract: Abstract In the Congo Free State, where the administration of Leopold II concentrated on economic exploitation and largely neglected family law, Belgian missionaries assumed functions the state left unattended. This article examines how they became legal actors in the regulation of marriage between 1885 and 1908, imposing monogamy as a condition of Christian and civilized life against the widespread practice of polygamy. Officiating marriages, keeping civil registers, adjudicating disputes over dowry, and organizing Catholic villages where monogamous unions were institutionalized, missionaries operated as intermediaries between the colonial administration and Congolese communities, their authority resting at once on canon law and on the practical demands of governance. Drawing on missionary periodicals, correspondence, decrees, and administrative records, the study reconstructs a legal role that has received little scholarly attention, situating it within debates on legal pluralism and vernacular imperial constitutionalism that treat law as a fluid practice articulated by diverse actors rather than a fixed body of metropolitan rules. By placing missionaries at the center of colonial lawmaking, the article shows how religion and law were interwoven in the making of the colonial state, even as local communities resisted and reshaped the norms imposed upon them. In conclusion, this study reveals the complexities of missionary involvement in colonial governance and offers new insights into the intersection of law, religion, and colonialism in Central Africa.
items.title: Filling the Legal Void: Missionaries as Legal Actors in Regulating Monogamous Unions in the Congo Free State (1885–1908)

items.abstract: Abstract The court of the marshalsea, which originated in the late thirteenth century, exercised jurisdiction over a circular area of twelve miles’ radius centered on the king’s current residence. This article offers the first scholarly discussion of this mysterious court in the reign of Henry VIII. It begins by discussing the court’s criminal jurisdiction and its judicial procedure in felony cases, explaining the significance of a 1542 statute that expanded and clarified its jurisdiction over serious crimes committed within the palace precinct. The article then analyzes the court’s civil jurisdiction and suggests reasons why its officers may have been willing to stretch jurisdictional rules in cases of trespass. Next, the article discusses what is known about the personnel of the court, charting the rise of the under-steward of the marshalsea (referred to as steward from 1539) as its chief controlling officer. I show that by 1542, the court’s jurisdiction had become trifurcated into a plea side, an ordinary criminal side, and a “palace” criminal side. Reforms to the court in the reign of Henry VIII illustrate a general process of judicial regularization that occurred in the early sixteenth century. The regularization of legal institutions during Henry’s reign was a “reformation from within” that promised to be far less destructive than the “reformation from without” forced on the marshalsea and other legal institutions under the Stuarts.
items.title: Law and Justice in the Court of the Marshalsea of the King’s Household, 1509–1547
Samuel Fury Childs Daly, Soldier’s Paradise: Militarism in Africa after Empire. Durham and London: Duke University Press, 2024. Pp. xiii + 297. $28.95 paperback. (ISBN 978-1-4780-3083-6)

items.abstract: Prevailing approaches to the contractual enforceability of modifications revise or dispense with the requirement of consideration and invoke economic duress to rule out unfair, inequitable, or bad faith modifications. Enforceability turns effectively on the absence of economic duress. But economic duress is a doctrine of avoidance.
